articles.title: CEVA Logistics opens new 50,000 m² warehouse in Italy
articles.summary: CEVA Logistics has opened a new 50,000-square-metre logistics hub in Castel San Giovanni, near Piacenza, Italy. The facility will support the operations of Daikin, expanding the logistics partnership between the two companies. The new warehouse is located in one of Italy’s main logistics corridors. articles.body: CEVA Logistics has opened a new 50,000-square-metre logistics hub in Castel San Giovanni, near Piacenza, Italy. The facility will support the operations of Daikin, expanding the logistics partnership between the two companies. The new warehouse is located in one of Italy’s main logistics corridors. It will provide additional capacity for Daikin while supporting its future business growth and distribution requirements. The opening also strengthens CEVA’s contract logistics network in Italy. The company now operates 33 facilities across the country, covering a total area of 526,000 square metres. The new site follows the expansion of CEVA’s partnership with Daikin in Spain. Earlier in 2026, the logistics provider opened a 27,000-square-metre warehouse in Tórtola de Henares to support the company’s operations. New facility strengthens European logistics network The Castel San Giovanni hub will help CEVA manage Daikin’s logistics requirements through additional warehouse capacity and flexible operational services. Its location near Piacenza provides access to an established transport and distribution corridor. This will support cargo movements across the Italian market. According to CEVA, the new facility will also allow the company to adjust its operations as customer volumes increase. “The opening of our new logistics hub in Castel San Giovanni marks an important milestone in the expansion of our contract logistics activities in Italy,” said Claudio Boschetti, Contract Logistics Product Head, Italy, CEVA Logistics. Boschetti added that the new site will provide additional capacity while supporting a gradual transition of operations. The facility operates under a multi-year lease agreement with CTP, the owner and developer of the property. The agreement supports CEVA’s long-term presence at the site as it continues developing its contract logistics activities in Italy. The latest opening adds to the company’s European warehousing network and strengthens its relationship with Daikin across multiple markets.

articles.title: ITF joins ISF Verify initiative to expand digital seafarer certification
articles.summary: The International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF) has joined the ISF Verify initiative, supporting efforts to expand digital seafarer certification across the global shipping industry. The agreement was signed during Hong Kong Maritime Week on 17 November 2026, bringing the ITF into a project developed by the...
articles.body: The International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF) has joined the ISF Verify initiative, supporting efforts to expand digital seafarer certification across the global shipping industry. The agreement was signed during Hong Kong Maritime Week on 17 November 2026, bringing the ITF into a project developed by the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) and Lloyd’s Register OneOcean. Through the cooperation, the initiative will gain access to the ITF’s seafarer network, which reaches approximately one million seafarers across more than 100 countries. The ITF and its inspectorate will also provide feedback to help ensure that the platform meets the practical needs of seafarers. Expanding access to digital certification ISF Verify is a cloud-based platform designed to replace paper-based certification processes with secure digital verification. The system connects seafarers, maritime administrations, port state control authorities and shipping companies, allowing certificates to be shared, checked and endorsed electronically. A key feature is that seafarers retain control over access to their personal information. They can decide who can view their certificate data and withdraw permission when necessary. The platform also operates as a connector between existing certification systems rather than a central database. Original certificate records remain with the issuing maritime authorities. The initiative aims to reduce administrative requirements while improving the efficiency of certificate verification across international shipping. “Digitalisation must work for seafarers – and that means ensuring that seafarers’ voices are heard so that we know that this technology will make their working lives easier through straightforward, secure and accessible certification,” said Stephen Cotton, General Secretary, International Transport Workers’ Federation. Cotton highlighted the role of ITF inspectors in gathering feedback from seafarers during the platform’s development. Initiative builds on progress in India and the Philippines The latest agreement follows the participation of India’s Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) earlier in November. India joined the initiative to explore connecting its national certification system with ISF Verify through a technical integration programme. The project has also completed a proof of concept with the Philippines’ Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA), creating a foundation for further implementation. Together, India and the Philippines represent approximately 30% of the global seafarer workforce, according to the ICS. However, their participation does not mean that all seafarers in those countries are already using the platform. “The industry needs a single, trusted connector that respects national jurisdiction authority while removing needless paper burden,” said Thomas A. Kazakos, Secretary General, International Chamber of Shipping. The ITF’s involvement is expected to provide additional input as the project moves towards wider international adoption. Under the initiative’s proposed operating model, seafarers will continue to have free access to their certificates through the mobile application. The partners have not announced a timetable for completing the global rollout.

articles.title: Seatrium secures MODEC contract for Hammerhead FPSO in Guyana

articles.body: Seatrium has secured a contract from MODEC for integration work on the Essequibo 1899 Floating Production, Storage and Offloading (FPSO) vessel, which will operate offshore Guyana. The contract covers the FPSO being developed for the Hammerhead offshore project. It marks Seatrium’s second FPSO integration project for MODEC in Guyana. Under the agreement, Seatrium will integrate topside modules and fabricate the vessel’s flare tower and crane pedestal. The company will also provide support during pre-commissioning and commissioning activities. The financial value of the contract and the expected completion date were not disclosed. FPSO designed for offshore Guyana operations The Essequibo 1899 will have an initial oil production capacity of approximately 150,000 barrels per day. The vessel will also incorporate gas and water handling systems and is designed to operate in water depths of approximately 1,025 metres. The new contract follows Seatrium’s completion of topside installation and integration work on the Errea Wittu FPSO. That vessel recently arrived in Guyana for deployment at the Uaru offshore development. “This award reinforces Seatrium’s position as the preferred integration partner for complex FPSO projects,” said Marlin Khiew, Executive Vice President of Seatrium Energy (Projects) and President, LATAM. Khiew added that the company’s experience from previous projects would support the execution of further FPSO integration work for MODEC. The latest award extends the relationship between the two companies as offshore energy infrastructure development continues in Guyana. Seatrium provides specialised engineering services across offshore energy, marine construction and vessel conversion projects. The Singapore-listed company operates an international network of shipyards and engineering facilities.

articles.title: How to Reduce False Positives in Vessel Screening Without Missing Real Risk
articles.summary: Screening Alerts Are a Volume Problem Before They Are Anything Else Every compliance team that touches maritime trade runs vessels through a screening system before a transaction proceeds. The system checks the vessel against sanctions lists, looks at its recent movements, flags anything that resembles a risk...
articles.body: How to Reduce False Positives in Vessel Screening Without Missing Real Risk in International Shipping News 18/11/2026 Screening Alerts Are a Volume Problem Before They Are Anything Else Every compliance team that touches maritime trade runs vessels through a screening system before a transaction proceeds. The system checks the vessel against sanctions lists, looks at its recent movements, flags anything that resembles a risk indicator, and produces an alert. An alert is a referral, not a finding. It says a human should look at this. Someone then investigates, decides whether the concern is real, and records the outcome. That process works when the alerts are mostly real. It breaks when they are not. A false positive is an alert that fires on a vessel doing nothing wrong. Every one of them consumes analyst time that produces no risk finding, and in a high-volume book they arrive faster than a team can clear them – which spawns alert fatigue. And the usual response is to adjust the system’s sensitivity threshold, meaning the level of suspicion required before an alert fires. Raise the threshold and fewer alerts fire. Fewer false positives, and also fewer true ones. That trade-off is real, and it is the wrong trade-off, because it treats a precision problem as a volume problem. A screening system producing false positives at scale cannot reliably distinguish a vessel that looks like a risk from a vessel that is one. Moving the threshold changes how many of each you see. It does not improve the system’s ability to tell them apart. Telling them apart requires context. Not only what the AIS record shows, but what the vessel has done over time, who owns it through how many layers, how its behavior compares to vessels confirmed as illicit, and whether the data source that triggered the alert is even reliable in the environment where the event occurred. A sensitivity setting supplies none of that. The Noise Has Specific Causes False positives in vessel screening are not randomly distributed across the fleet. They cluster around four specific failures in the data the screening system reads, and each one produces a recognizable kind of bad alert. The first is data that describes events that never happened. The second is missing data read as deliberate concealment. The third is a vessel’s identity changing faster than the screening record. The fourth is correct behavior that looks wrong without context. Each needs a different answer, and none of them is a threshold. The first failure is the least intuitive, because the data is not missing. It is present, detailed, and describes something that did not occur. GPS Jamming Generates Activity That Never Happened In a GPS-jammed area, injected coordinates place vessels at positions they never occupied. The system records a port call, a meeting, or a proximity event, and the screening engine treats it as real. Across a single week of concentrated jamming in the Middle East Gulf, Windward removed 2,056 port calls across 845 vessels and 20,848 meetings across 695 vessels, none of which occurred. Gulf jamming landscape in the Middle East Gulf, March 2026. Red hexagons mark injection zones, where vessels report positions they never occupied. Yellow marks denial zones, where AIS is silenced. Source: Windward Maritime AI™ Platform. The second failure is the opposite. The data is absent, and the screening system reads the absence as intent. AIS Gaps Get Read As Deliberate Dark Activity A vessel loses signal in a congested port and the alert fires as though it went dark on purpose. In the Middle East Gulf, switching off AIS has become normal practice rather than a red flag. Windward recorded dark convoy passages accounting for 47% of Strait of Hormuz transits in August 2026 and 52% in September, as vessels crossed with AIS off for crew and vessel safety. A screening model treating every gap in that corridor as concealment would flag the majority of legitimate traffic. Compliance teams tell us this is where much of their Iran-related false positive volume comes from. Vessels switch off AIS for crew and vessel safety rather than for concealment. The third failure is not about the data being wrong. It is about the screening system matching against the wrong vessel. Identity Changes Break the Match A vessel that changes flag, name, or MMSI can trigger screening against its former registration rather than its current one, or be confused with a different vessel carrying a similar history. The fourth failure involves no data error at all. The record is accurate, and the alert is still wrong. Legitimate Transits Look Like Approaches A vessel routed correctly past a sanctioned port appears suspicious without route context. The alert describes proximity. It does not describe intent, destination, or whether the vessel ever stopped. None of these four is a tuning problem. Each comes from what the screening system is reading, or failing to read, which means each has an answer in the data rather than in the sensitivity setting. Context Resolves What a Trigger Cannot What separates a real alert from a false one is almost always something outside the event that triggered it. The vessel’s own past behavior, the behavior of comparable vessels, and whether the physical facts support what the record claims. A screening system that evaluates each event in isolation cannot reach any of that. One that compares the event against the vessel’s history can. Take the GPS jamming case. A port call recorded in an area with active jamming during the arrival hour is suspect. A port call recorded in that same area by a vessel that has made clean, unjammed visits to that port in the preceding six months is probably real. One clean historical visit is enough to validate the current call. That single comparison separates a manufactured event from a genuine one without any analyst touching it. The same logic applies across the other categories. A speed and distance feasibility check establishes whether an alleged port call was physically possible given the vessel’s known positions before and after. Ownership network analysis surfaces whether a beneficial owner shows a pattern of association with sanctioned entities across a fleet rather than on the single hull being screened. Pattern-of-life analysis built on multi-year behavior distinguishes a vessel making an unusual call from a vessel behaving in a way that is structurally consistent with illicit trade. None of these reduce sensitivity. They replace a binary trigger with a calibrated assessment, which is a different thing entirely. The Cost of Getting This Wrong Is Measurable The effect shows up in two directions. One major energy company reported to Windward, self-rejecting 46 to 50% of vessels under evaluation, losing business to competitors as a result, and running a recurring three-day manual exercise every two weeks to pre-approve a list of roughly 5,000 vessels using several data sources in parallel. Its compliance team described difficulty justifying those rejections to senior management without better data behind them. That is the business cost. The compliance cost runs the other way. For one customer over a twelve-month period, removing GPS jamming-generated activity lowered the risk score on approximately 495 vessels. Around 260 moved from High to Low, 160 from High to Moderate, and 75 from Moderate to Low. Those were not borderline calls being softened. They were vessels carrying elevated risk scores built on events that had not occurred. A compliance team working that book is not just seeing too many alerts. It is prioritizing against a risk ranking that is wrong. Clearing an Alert Is a Documentation Problem There is a regulatory argument underneath the efficiency one, and for compliance leads it is the more important of the two. When a team clears a vessel, the question a regulator asks later is not whether it was screened. It is how the determination was reached that it was not a risk. “AIS showed it was not in a sanctioned port” is a thin answer, particularly if the AIS record in question came from a jamming-affected corridor. A multi-sensor assessment is a materially stronger one. The vessel’s AIS showed proximity to the terminal, satellite imagery showed it anchored offshore with no draft change consistent with discharge, its ownership chain resolved clean across seven layers, and its behavior over eighteen months shows no prior association with sanctioned terminals. That resolves in minutes rather than hours, and more importantly, it leaves a record of why the decision was made rather than only that it was. One further point worth stating. Not every alert that clears was a false positive. A genuine designated-vessel encounter can be cleared on the strength of a specific license and supporting documentation, and that is a correct finding, not a system error. The distinction matters for how a team measures itself. Counting cleared alerts as noise will push a program toward exactly the threshold-raising it should be avoiding. Fewer Alerts Is the Byproduct, Not the Goal The objective is not a quieter queue. A quieter queue is achievable in an afternoon by moving a slider, and the cost arrives later. The objective is that each alert reaching an analyst carries enough context to be resolved with confidence, and that each clearance leaves a record capable of surviving external review. Volume falls out of that as a consequence. A screening system that fires on what a vessel appears to have done will keep producing noise, because appearance is what deceptive operators control. A system that assesses what a vessel has actually done, across time and across sources, produces fewer alerts and better ones. Source: Windward 2026-11-18 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: The system checks the vessel against sanctions lists, looks at its recent movements, flags anything that resembles a risk indicator, and produces an alert.
An alert is a referral, not a finding.
It says a human should look at this.

articles.body: Newbuilding Activity Shows Signs of “Fatigue” in Hellenic Shipping News 18/11/2026 A fter weeks of growth, newbuilding activity has slowed down last week. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Banchero Costa said that “newbuilding activity this week was somewhat more subdued, with 28 vessels reported across a broad range of sectors. Despite the lower number of contracts, activity remained well distributed, with notable orders in the bulk carrier, container, car carrier, tanker and gas carrier sectors. Tanker ordering continued to attract attention, with a new VLCC joining the orderbook, while several singlevessel contracts were also reported across different segments. In the bulk carrier sector, Leon Shipping & Trading reportedly contracted 1x 84,000 dwt bulk carrier at Hengli Heavy Industries, China, with delivery scheduled for June 2029. Nomikos also reportedly placed an order for 1x 82,000 dwt bulk carrier at Oshima Shipbuilding, Japan, with delivery scheduled for March 2030. No pricing details were disclosed for either contract”. The shipbroker added that “tanker ordering continued across the crude oil and chemical segments. DHT Holdings reportedly contracted 1x 320,000 dwt VLCC at Hanwha Ocean, South Korea. In the chemical sector, two 40,000 dwt stainless steel chemical tankers were reportedly contracted at Kitanihon Shipbuilding, Japan, at approximately USD 72.5 million each, with deliveries scheduled for June 2029. Although the contracting owner remains undisclosed, both vessels are understood to be intended for charter to Odfjell, Norway, with a probable purchase option. In the container sector, Eastern Pacific Shipping reportedly contracted 4x 9,000 teu containerships at Imabari Shipbuilding, Japan. Deliveries are scheduled in two pairs, with the first two vessels expected in June 2030 and the remaining two in December 2031. The vessels will be conventionally fuelled. Car carrier activity was particularly notable, with Global Car Carriers reportedly contracting 4x PCTCs across two separate shipbuilding programmes. The first 2 vessels are scheduled for delivery in October and December 2030 and will be the first car carriers constructed at Zhoushan Changhong International. A further 2 vessels were contracted at China Merchants Weihai, with deliveries scheduled for June and December 2031. The latter vessels will each have an 8,600-car capacity and feature LNG dual-fuel propulsion, with an option to switch to ammonia. In the gas carrier sector, Thenamaris reportedly contracted 2x 174,000 cu.m. LNG carriers at Hyundai, South Korea, priced at approximately USD 243.7 million each, with deliveries scheduled for December 2030. Foresight Group also reportedly contracted 1x 90,000 cu.m. LPG/ammonia carrier at Hyundai, priced at approximately USD 117.5 million, with delivery scheduled for October 2029”, Banchero Costa concluded. Meanwhile, in the S&P market, shipbroker Xclusiv said that “in dry bulk, activity was spread across all sizes. On the Post-Panamax sector, the “Shun Chang” – 93K/2010 Yangfan Group was sold for low/mid USD 15 mills, while the “Auriga Ocean” – 94K/2008 Namura changed hands for excess USD 15 mills. Moving down the sizes, the Kamsarmax “Taho Australia” – 82K/2019 Oshima was sold for very high USD 38 mills. On the Panamax sector, Chinese buyers acquired the “Tariel” – 77K/2001 Imabari for USD 8 mills. On the Supramax sector, clients of Fujian Highton acquired the “Kang Cheng” – 56K/2004 NACKS for USD 11.55 mills. The Handysize sector saw significant activity, with the “Jinling Confidence” – 40K/2017 Nanjing Dongze and the “Nanjing Confidence” – 40K/2017 Nanjing Dongze sold en bloc for USD 24 mills each. On the same sector, Turkish buyers acquired the “Danae” – 40K/2022 Shin Kurushima for USD 34.5 mills, while the logger “African Owl” – 34K/2016 Namura changed hands for excess USD 22 mills. The “Lucky Voyager” – 37K/2009 Saiki was sold for USD 14.5 mills, while the “UBC Santos” – 32K/2008 Saiki found new owners for USD 11.5 mills. Finally, the “ABK Tiger” – 28K/2002 Imabari was sold for around USD 5.3 mills, the “East Wind I” – 28K/2002 Imabari for USD 5.85 mills and the “Duyen Hai 1” – 28K/2001 Kanda for around USD 5.5 mills”. Source: Xclusiv shipbroker “On the VLCC sector, clients of ADNOC acquired the scrubber fitted “Olympic Lady” – 300K/2017 Hyundai for USD 185 mills. Moving down the sizes, the Suezmax shuttle tanker “Jasmine Knutsen” – 149K/2005 Samsung was sold for a conversion. On the smaller tanker sizes, the stainless steel “Taruca” – 20K/2005 Fukuoka changed hands for mid/high USD 12 mills, while Indonesian buyers acquired the “Bagshot” – 18K/2023 Hyundai Mipo for USD 37.25 mills. On the same sector, the “Elisabeth Schulte” – 16K/2010 Jiangzhou was sold for an undisclosed price, while the “Sinar Busan” – 11K/2006 STX found new owners for USD 7.5 mills”, Xclusiv concluded. articles.body: Gulf Earnings Give Way as VLCC Ballasters Build East of Suez in International Shipping News 18/11/2026 I n Week 46, freight weakness spread to Gulf routes, following a Week 45 correction that had primarily impacted the Atlantic (where Gulf VLCC earnings dropped under 5%). East of Suez, average ballast VLCC counts rose from 415 to 434 vessels, while laden VLCC counts fell from 341 to 321. Consequently, the ballast surplus expanded from 74 to 114 vessels, over triple the Q3 2026 average of 37, in sharp contrast to the same period in 2025, when laden vessels held a slight majority over ballasters. Ballast VLCCs East of Suez surged to 450 by 12 November, marking their highest count since late March, against 308 laden vessels. Chart 1. VLCCs East of Suez in ballast and laden, daily, January–12 November 2026, and the average ballast surplus (ballast minus laden) over selected windows. Source: Signal Ocean vessel positions The rise in ballast VLCCs East of Suez coincided with a 17.9% weekly decline in Middle East Gulf–China (TD3C) earnings to $1.06 million/day on 13 November. However, the growing ballast count does not necessarily mean more vessels are available for prompt Gulf employment. Actual availability remains constrained by vessel positioning, existing charter commitments, and owners’ willingness to accept Gulf voyages. VLCC Earnings: The Gulf Follows the Atlantic US Gulf–China (TD22) earnings fell 44.1% over the week to $232,000/day on 13 November. TD3C lost about $230,000/day, more than the $183,000/day lost by TD22, but TD22’s larger percentage fall lifted the TD3C/TD22 ratio from 3.10 on 6 November to 4.55, its highest level since 6 May. Chart 2. Daily TD3C and TD22 TCE assessments and their ratio, 14 November 2025–13 November 2026. Shading marks 9–13 November.Source: Baltic Exchange assessments via Signal Ocean. Daily TCEs derived from the Signal Ocean TD3C/TD22 differential series through 12 November and the route assessments for 13 November. Both VLCC routes have retreated substantially from their 8 October peaks, with TD3C earnings down 25.2% and TD22 down 63.6% by 13 November. TD3C reached its lowest level since 14 September, while TD22 fell to its lowest since 9 September. Despite the sharper percentage decline in Atlantic earnings, the absolute earnings gap between the two routes narrowed to $824,000/day, from $871,000/day on 6 November. Weekly-average comparison: 9–13 November against 2–6 November, five assessment days each. Arithmetic means of daily observations; the ratio row averages daily ratios. MARKET SIGNAL: Gulf VLCC earnings declined in Week 46, although the correction was sharper on Atlantic routes. The TD3C/TD22 earnings ratio widened to 4.55 on 13 November, driven by the steeper fall in Atlantic earnings rather than stronger Gulf rates. Cargo demand and vessel positioning across both basins will remain key to the direction of freight rates. Freight: Gulf Routes Join the Largest Declines All 16 dirty routes fell between 6 and 13 November. The largest declines were on US Gulf–China VLCC (TD22, -44.1%), West Africa–China VLCC (TD15, -43.7%), Black Sea–Mediterranean Suezmax (TD6, -35.9%) and North Sea–Continent Aframax (TD7, -35.8%). Unlike Week 45, four of the ten largest declines were on routes loading East of Suez: Southeast Asia–East Coast Australia Aframax (TD14, -32.1%), MEG–Singapore VLCC (TD2, -18.9%), MEG–China VLCC (TD3C, -17.9%) and Kuwait–Singapore Aframax (TD8, -14.7%). MEG–Mediterranean Suezmax (TD23) recorded the smallest decline, at 2.6%. Weekly losses on several Atlantic Aframax routes were smaller than in Week 45, at between 6% and 10% for US Gulf–ARA (TD25), Cross-Mediterranean (TD19), Caribbean–US Gulf (TD9) and East Coast Mexico–US Gulf (TD26). On 13 November alone, TD25 rose 9.2%, TD26 5.6%, TD9 4.9% and West Africa–China VLCC 3.6%; a single assessment day does not establish a change in direction. Chart 3. Crude tanker TCE, percentage change from 6 to 13 November, by loading area.Source: Baltic Exchange TCE assessments via Signal Ocean. Weekly change is point-to-point from the 6 November reference. Supply: Ballast and Laden Positions by Segment VLCCs. West of Suez, average ballast VLCC counts increased by 7.0% to 76.4 vessels, while laden counts declined by 3.4% to 72.0. The balance shifted from a laden surplus of three vessels to a ballast surplus of four, with the ballast-to-laden ratio rising from 0.96 to 1.06. Ballast VLCCs have outnumbered laden vessels daily since 4 November, although the ratio remains below the Q3 2026 average of 1.15 and the 1.14 recorded a year earlier. Both ballast and laden counts remain 16–21% below the corresponding week of 2025. East of Suez, the ratio increased from 1.22 to 1.35, above the Q3 average of 1.11 and 0.99 a year earlier, with ballast VLCC counts up 27% year-on-year. Suezmax and Aframax/LR2. West of Suez, laden Suezmaxes continued to outnumber ballasters, although the gap narrowed from 35 to 27 vessels as laden counts declined by 2.7% to 235. The ballast-to-laden ratio stood at 0.89, below the Q3 average of 1.06. East of Suez, Suezmax ballast counts rose 3.0% to 158.9, bringing the ratio to 1.22, close to the Q3 average of 1.24. For Aframax/LR2s West of Suez, laden counts rose by 2.3% to 367.7, up 32% year-on-year, reaching 377 vessels on 12 November, the highest daily level since January 2023. The ballast-to-laden ratio remained at 0.88, below the Q3 average of 1.10. East of Suez, laden Aframax/LR2 counts declined by 4.0% to 285.4, leaving ballast and laden populations virtually equal. Changes in vessels and per cent; a positive ballast-laden figure means ballast vessels outnumber laden ones. Aframax/LR2 is a combined size category. Chart 4. Ballast and laden vessels West and East of Suez, daily, VLCC, Suezmax and Aframax/LR2, 1 September–12 November 2026.Source: Signal Ocean vessel positions and draft status. The wider VLCC fleet remains concentrated East of Suez: the East/West ratio stood at 5.11 on 12 November, slightly below its 2026 high of 5.19 on 3 November, compared with 3.77 in 2025 and 3.25 in 2024. Fleet Distribution and Repositioning While the ballast VLCC population East of Suez increased during Week 46, the latest fleet distribution shows a modest rise in vessels positioned West of Suez. The western VLCC count increased from 131 to 141 over five days, while the eastern count eased from its 4 November peak of 641 to 629. Nevertheless, about 82% of the fleet remained East of Suez, up from a typical 75%. Active westbound VLCC ballasters declined slightly from 49 to 47, including 39 originating in the Far East. Brazil remained the leading destination with 20 vessels, followed by South Africa with nine. Suezmax positioning continued to shift East, with the eastern fleet increasing from 232 vessels in mid-October to 264 on 14 November, representing approximately 42% of the fleet against a typical 35%. Active westbound Suezmax ballasters declined from 51 to 46. Aframax ballasters increased marginally from 60 to 61, including 29 heading towards the US Gulf and ten towards Argentina and Uruguay. The US Gulf Aframax tonnage list stood at 39 vessels on 14 November, compared with an average of approximately 50 in September. Chart 5. Active westbound VLCC, Suezmax and Aframax ballasters, previous update vs 15 November, and destination mix. Active counts represent vessels in transit rather than immediately available tonnage.Source: Signal Maritime Key Insights, 8 and 15 November 2026. Previous update: VLCC and Suezmax 8 November, Aframax 7 November. “Other destinations” is the segment total minus the listed destinations. Signal Maritime fleet counts use a different vessel population from the Signal Ocean position data above. US Gulf Loadings and Atlantic Demand US Gulf crude loadings reached 125.5 million barrels in October, up 18% from September, with the daily average increasing by 14% to approximately 4.0 million b/d. During 1–12 November, tracked loadings averaged 3.1 million b/d, although the figure remains provisional and covers only the first 12 days of the month. The slower pace of US Gulf loadings in early November came alongside an increase in Atlantic ballast tonnage and further declines in VLCC earnings. While fewer cargoes may have contributed to the softer freight market, the growing ballast supply and weaker fixing sentiment also played a role, making it difficult to attribute the correction to cargo demand alone. Chart 6. VLCC fleet East/West ratio by calendar day, 2024–2026, and US Gulf tracked crude loadings, monthly average in million b/d, 2024–2026, with provisional 1–12 November 2026. Volumes include all destinations and vessel sizes.Sources: Signal Ocean Fleet Distribution; Signal Ocean cargo flows by loading date. November 2026 data are provisional. The decline in Atlantic VLCC freight rates has reduced the transportation-cost component of long-haul crude shipments to Asia, potentially improving the relative economics of West African and Brazilian cargoes. However, the extent of any improvement in delivered competitiveness also depends on crude-grade price differentials and refinery demand. The key freight consideration is whether lower voyage costs encourage additional Atlantic-to-Asia cargo movements, providing employment for vessels already positioned in the Atlantic Basin. Hormuz Freight Watch: Macro Risks Security risks continue to weigh on tanker operations in the Gulf. The Joint Maritime Information Center’s 12 November advisory recorded further projectile strikes on tankers in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz on 10–11 November. Repeated attacks continue to restrict the pool of owners willing to accept Gulf employment, while elevated war-risk insurance costs and operational delays add to voyage expenses and limit effective vessel availability. Meanwhile, the recovery in Middle East oil production and exports is changing the cargo outlook. The IEA’s 13 November assessment projects a 1.7 million b/d global oil supply surplus in Q4, the first since the conflict began, although further attacks on shipping could disrupt the recovery. OPEC’s November report places October crude production among participating OPEC+ countries at 41.23 million b/d, up approximately 2.04 million b/d from September, based on secondary sources. Higher Middle East exports could support additional tanker employment, although continued security risks and limited owner participation in Gulf trades may constrain the impact on freight. Seven OPEC+ producers are scheduled to meet on 29 November. Key Takeaways The Week 46 correction extended across both Atlantic and Gulf VLCC markets, although Atlantic earnings experienced the sharper percentage decline. East of Suez, the growing ballast population points to a change in vessel positioning, but does not establish an equivalent increase in commercially available Gulf tonnage. The next test will be whether additional cargo requirements absorb vessels repositioning across both basins. The pace of Atlantic long-haul employment, Gulf loading activity and owners’ willingness to accept regional risks will remain central to the freight balance. articles.title: Clean Shipping Alliance Disappointed on Greenland’s scrubber ban
articles.summary: We are disappointed to see Greenland announce restrictions on exhaust gas cleaning systems (EGCS, or “scrubbers”), starting in 2027. Of course, protecting the Arctic’s sensitive marine environment is important, no question. What we haven’t yet understood, though, is what specific risk Greenland has identified from...
articles.body: Clean Shipping Alliance Disappointed on Greenland’s scrubber ban in International Shipping News 18/11/2026 We are disappointed to see Greenland announce restrictions on exhaust gas cleaning systems (EGCS, or “scrubbers”), starting in 2027. Of course, protecting the Arctic’s sensitive marine environment is important, no question. What we haven’t yet understood, though, is what specific risk Greenland has identified from EGCS in its waters, and how that risk was assessed. The IMO’s MEPC.1/Circ.899 provides an agreed method for evaluating local risk, including the receiving environment, discharge composition, dilution and ecotoxicity. If Greenland has conducted an assessment to support its planned restrictions, we urge them to publish it. If no assessment has been conducted under these guidelines, the case for the restrictions has not been established through the IMO’s framework. A precautionary approach – which is likely the case in Greenland, as in most other places with scrubber restrictions — cannot replace the assessment that the IMO framework calls for. The IMO’s risk characterization and assessment are conducted using the same or similar internationally accepted methods that many countries use to evaluate the acceptability of other discharges for licensing. These IMO-aligned assessments therefore use processes familiar to technical experts in each country. Where these assessments have been carried out, the recently published, peer-reviewed Puget Sound study being one example, they have found low or negligible risk under real operating conditions. That is no surprise, it just reinforces the importance of assessing discharges in context. What would be a surprise is if there is an announced restriction before there has been any assessment of EGCS in Greenland’s waters. Andreas Chrysostomou Greenland’s plans would extend restrictions to territorial seas, beyond OSPAR’s current recommendation, and add closed-loop and hybrid systems from 2029. Operators are entitled to know what the restrictions are based on and what specific risk each phase addresses, with different systems and operating modes assessed on their own evidence. The call for the IMO to adopt a global ban, starting in the Arctic, is ultimately a call to change international regulation. Regrettably, Greenland is not alone, and most, if not all, countries with existing EGCS restrictions have also not conducted an IMO-aligned evaluation. We must conclude that these decisions are not based solely on recognized science. Regulation 4 of MARPOL Annex VI recognises EGCS as an equivalent means of compliance. If governments want to change that, the proper route is a transparent amendment at the IMO, supported by location-specific evidence, not a series of regional bans that pre-empt the discussion at PPR 14. The most common objection is that scrubbers simply move pollution from air to sea. In reality, EGCS remove sulphur and other substances from exhaust gases, reducing their release to air, where they pose the greatest health risk, and depositing them to sea, where they are already naturally present and quickly revert to background concentrations. EGCS can also significantly reduce particulate matter in exhaust emissions, as well as PAHs and metals. This is particularly relevant near land, including in ports and harbours. The same substances found in scrubber discharge are also present in the air emissions of non-EGCS ships. This means proposals such as the Nuuk-Reykjavik green corridor, which would rely on MGO, are not an impact-free alternative. In fact, CE Delft’s 2021 well-to-wake analysis found that refining MGO increases lifecycle CO2 emissions by 10-25%, while operating EGCS adds 1.0-1.5%. A 2025 well-to-wake study submitted to the IMO as PPR 13/INF.6 found that HFO used with EGCS delivers equal or lower overall environmental impacts than VLSFO and MGO across most categories. A green corridor relying on MGO therefore cannot be assumed to deliver a better overall environmental outcome than continued EGCS use, including for the marine environment. Assessments should compare complete fuel pathways, not a visible discharge against an alternative assumed to have no impact. Source: By Andreas Chrysostomou, Executive Director, Clean Shipping Alliance 2026-11-18 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Of course, protecting the Arctic’s sensitive marine environment is important, no question.
What we haven’t yet understood, though, is what specific risk Greenland has identified from EGCS in its waters, and how that risk was assessed.
The IMO’s MEPC.1/Circ.899 provides an agreed method for evaluating local risk, including the receiving environment, discharge composition, dilution and ecotoxicity.

articles.title: Black Sea Grain Trade Shifts to the Baltic
articles.summary: Ukraine and Russia are often called the breadbasket of the world because of their fertile soil and their key role in the global food supply chain. When the war in Ukraine broke out worries about Black Sea grain supply followed, yet grain exports from the region have remained largely intact. Recently, however, attacks...
articles.body: Black Sea Grain Trade Shifts to the Baltic in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 18/11/2026 U kraine and Russia are often called the breadbasket of the world because of their fertile soil and their key role in the global food supply chain. When the war in Ukraine broke out worries about Black Sea grain supply followed, yet grain exports from the region have remained largely intact. Recently, however, attacks on merchant vessels and port infrastructure in the Black Sea have escalated sharply. This has led to damaged infrastructure and pushed shipowners to avoid the area, which has significantly reduced Black Sea grain trade. According to Shipfix data, grain cargoes circulated for loading in the Black Sea from August to October totaled 61.4 million tonnes, down 43% from the same period last year. This is a detrimental drop, considering October normally falls within the peak grain export season, driven by the northern hemisphere harvest. A decline of this size typically dulls shipping demand and does not bode well for dry bulk freight rates. However, this has not entirely been the case in this region, with some of these volumes redirected overland to be exported out of the Baltic Sea from July to October 2026. This has been particularly evident for Russia, which has ports in both the Black Sea and the Baltic Sea. As a result, grain cargoes circulated for loading in the Baltic from August to October 2026 reached 36.3 million tonnes, up 43% from last year. How will this shift impact dry bulk freight rates? This shift in the grain trade offers a silver lining for dry bulk freight markets. Most Black Sea grain is destined for the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, a sailing distance of around 1,000 to 2,000 nautical miles. From the Baltic, the average distance to the same area is around 4,000 nautical miles. The longer voyages increase ton-miles, which supports freight rates. The surge in Baltic grain shipments has also strained port capacity and caused congestion in the area. According to Oceanbolt data, the tonnage waiting to load in the Baltic more than doubled between July and October. This is an unusual development, adding further inefficiency to the market and providing additional support for freight rates. The shift in Russian grain exports is likely benefiting smaller vessels, while larger ones are left out in the cold. Handysizes carry about 56% of Baltic grain and Supramaxes 27%, but the Panamaxes only carry 4%. Panamaxes typically carry around 22% of Black Sea grain volumes, so they suffer from the drop in that trade. Yet they gain far less than Handysizes and Supramaxes from the diversion to the Baltic. This may partly explain the recent disparity in freight rates, with Panamax rates falling below both Supramax and Handysize. If this trading pattern continues, we may see this disparity persist in the near term with Supramaxes and Handysizes earning more than the Panamaxes. Source: Veson Nautical Tops 2026-11-18 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: ENGINE: East of Suez Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook in International Shipping News 18/11/2026 Singapore and Malaysia Bunker fuel availability remains tight in Singapore, with terminal loading schedules and barge capacity heavily booked for most suppliers throughout November. Some suppliers have already received bookings for dates in December, a source said. VLSFO lead times have increased to around 15-17 days, compared with 13-15 days last week. LSMGO lead times have also lengthened, rising to 12-14 days from 7-10 days previously. In contrast, HSFO lead times have shortened to 9-12 days from around 12-16 days last week. In Malaysia, bunker supply remains constrained across several fuel grades at Port Klang. Prompt VLSFO availability is particularly limited, while LSMGO supply remains tight and HSFO availability continues to be restricted. East Asia Bad weather has disrupted bunker deliveries in Zhoushan, leaving suppliers working through accumulated backlogs. Availability remains tight across all fuel grades, with lead times extending to around nine days. Supply conditions vary across other Chinese ports. Dalian and Qingdao have sufficient VLSFO and LSMGO stocks, although HSFO availability remains tight in Qingdao. All three grades are in tight supply in Tianjin, while VLSFO and HSFO supplies remain limited in Shanghai. LSMGO availability in Shanghai, however, is relatively stable. Supply constraints also persist in southern China, where suppliers in Fuzhou, Xiamen, Yangpu and Guangzhou are reporting shortages of both VLSFO and LSMGO. Bunker supply in Hong Kong remains stable, with suppliers recommending lead times of around seven days for the major fuel grades. In Taiwan, suppliers in Keelung, Taichung and Hualien are recommending lead times of around two days for VLSFO and LSMGO. Lead times in Kaohsiung are slightly longer at three days, remaining broadly unchanged from last week. Bunker demand has weakened across South Korea as prices remain higher than those at neighbouring bunkering hubs, according to a local trader. Busan’s VLSFO is currently priced at premiums of $79/mt over Singapore and $36/mt over Zhoushan. At southern ports, including Busan, Ulsan, Masan, Onsan, Yeosu and Kwangyang, lead times for all major fuel grades are around 3-7 days. Similar lead times apply to VLSFO, LSMGO and HSFO at western ports, including Incheon, Daesan, Dangjin, Pyeongtaek and Taean. However, adverse weather could disrupt bunker operations at several South Korean ports over the coming days. Operations in Busan and Ulsan may face disruptions until 19 November and from 21-25 November. Yeosu could experience disruptions on until 21 November and from 24-26 November, while Daesan may face interruptions from 18-21 and 23-26 November. Japan’s bunker market remains extremely tight, particularly for VLSFO, with availability continuing to deteriorate across major ports. Despite ongoing enquiries, Japanese refiners have yet to confirm their December supply allocations or issue firm offers for next month’s deliveries. November supply is virtually exhausted, leaving very few opportunities for new spot enquiries, a Japan-based trader said. In the Keihin area, covering Tokyo, Yokohama and Kawasaki, November supply slots are effectively fully booked, with suppliers unable to accommodate additional spot enquiries for VLSFO. Further offers for November deliveries are unlikely unless existing nominations are cancelled or previously allocated volumes become available. One supplier continues to face supply constraints following maintenance at Negishi refinery and requirements to transfer fuel domestically. Its availability is expected to remain restricted until around 24 November. Two other suppliers are also operating with extremely limited flexibility, leaving almost no room for additional spot volumes. VLSFO supply conditions are similarly challenging in western Japan, particularly in Nagoya, Osaka, Mizushima and Oita, where most suppliers have already committed their available November volumes. VLSFO availability remains severely constrained at several Japanese ports, including Tokyo, Chiba, Kawasaki, Nagoya, Yokkaichi, Osaka, Kobe, Mizushima, Tokuyama and Oita. Supplies at these locations are subject to enquiry. In contrast, HSFO and LSMGO availability remains normal. VLSFO and HSFO supplies are tight in Kashima. Indonesia remains an exception to the tighter supply conditions prevailing across much of East Asia, with bunker fuel availability generally healthy. Suppliers in Jakarta, Surabaya, Balikpapan and Cigading are typically recommending VLSFO lead times of just 2–3 days. Oceania Bunker fuel availability remains stable in Western Australia, with VLSFO readily available in Kwinana and Fremantle. Suppliers at both ports recommend lead times of around seven days. Each port has a single supplier, and all bunker deliveries are conducted by barge. Supply conditions are mixed along Australia’s east coast. Port Kembla has normal VLSFO availability, with deliveries possible by truck or pipeline. Sydney has sufficient VLSFO and LSMGO stocks, although HSFO availability is tighter and suppliers generally require around seven days’ notice. Brisbane and Gladstone have ample supplies of VLSFO and LSMGO, with lead times of approximately one week. VLSFO availability has also improved in Melbourne and Geelong. However, HSFO availability has tightened further in Melbourne and Brisbane. The cyclone season could pose risks to bunker operations across Australia, a source said. Running from November through April, the season has the potential to disrupt fuel availability at ports nationwide. New Zealand’s bunker market remains broadly stable, with VLSFO readily available in Tauranga and Auckland. Suppliers at both ports recommend lead times of around four days. At Marsden Point, vessels can receive VLSFO and LSMGO directly through pipelines. Adverse weather remains the main operational risk in New Zealand, particularly in Wellington and ports across the South Island, where disruptions to marine operations could delay bunker deliveries. In Papua New Guinea, LSMGO availability remains tight at Rabaul, Madang and Lae. South Asia Suppliers are recommending bunker lead times of around 2-3 days for all three major fuel grades at several key Indian ports, including Mumbai, Cochin, Paradip, Visakhapatnam, Kakinada, Haldia, Chennai, Tuticorin and New Mangalore, according to an India-based source. Adverse weather is forecast at Visakhapatnam between 17 and 21 November, potentially disrupting bunker operations and delaying deliveries. In Sri Lanka, lead times for all major fuel grades at Colombo are around 7-11 days. High waves are expected to affect bunkering operations at Trincomalee between 17 and 21 November. Middle East “The situation across the Middle East has improved slightly, and things have become relatively calmer. Port operations are gradually stabilising, with a more positive outlook compared to previous weeks,” a Middle East-based source said. Availability in Fujairah has improved this week, despite continued disruption to vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz amid US-Iran tensions. Last week, supplies were tight across all three major fuel grades, with limited availability for both prompt and forward deliveries. VLSFO lead times are currently around five days, with some suppliers still able to accommodate prompt deliveries. LSMGO and HSFO lead times stand at approximately seven days, although prompt availability remains limited for both grades, according to a regional source. In Saudi Arabia, LSMGO availability in Jeddah remains generally stable, while VLSFO supply continues to be tight. At Omani ports, including Salalah, Sohar, Duqm and Muscat, LSMGO deliveries can generally be arranged within 2–3 days. Supply of both VLSFO and LSMGO remains restricted at Qatar’s Ras Laffan. Meanwhile, Egypt’s Port Suez is experiencing low bunker inventories across all major fuel grades. Djibouti also continues to face limited availability of the three major bunker fuel grades. Source: By Tuhin Roy, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news 2026-11-18 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Fresh tanker attack in Hormuz highlights ongoing threats facing Gulf shipping in International Shipping News 18/11/2026 A new tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz has been reported by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre, in the latest of a string of incidents targeting vessels attempting to traverse the vital waterway. In a statement dated Monday, the British trade monitor said a third-party had reported that the attack had disabled the ship and sparked a fire in the engine room. The crew are reportedly safe, while the damage assessment and environmental impact of the attack was unknown. The UKMTO reiterated a recent warning that vessels should transit Hormuz with “caution.” Since November 10, the UKMTO has reported seven attacks in or near Hormuz, a key conduit for roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas before the outbreak of the Iran war in late February. The developments have left the status of the strait mired in uncertainty. Despite moves by Iran to stem traffic through Hormuz, shipping data have indicated that more tankers are making the sailing thanks in part to increase U.S. security in the region. Still, the attacks have sustained fears of possible disruptions to oil flows out of the Gulf region, while messaging around negotiations to end the Middle East conflict has been muddled. Fighting has also been intense in between Houthi rebels in Yemen and Saudi-backed coalition forces, particularly in battles in and around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical waterway for global shipping. These concerns have been a counterweight to recent forecasts that oil supplies will outstrip demand for the first time since the start of the Iran war. Benchmark Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, were last trading higher by 1.7% at $94.01 a barrel, although the contract has slid by more than 14% over the last one-month period. articles.summary: Lloyd’s Register (LR) has introduced new ship design requirements aimed at containing electric vehicle fires before they can spread through car carriers and RoRo vessels, addressing the particular safety challenges associated with transporting lithium-ion batteries at sea. The new FIRE (EV) special feature notation...
articles.body: Lloyd’s Register introduces new notation to tackle EV fire risks on car carriers in International Shipping News 18/11/2026 Lloyd’s Register (LR) has introduced new ship design requirements aimed at containing electric vehicle fires before they can spread through car carriers and RoRo vessels, addressing the particular safety challenges associated with transporting lithium-ion batteries at sea. The new FIRE (EV) special feature notation sets requirements covering fire detection, structural fire protection, ventilation, suppression and firefighting equipment and systems for ships carrying electric vehicles. It applies to RoRo and RoPax ships, Pure Car Carriers (PCCs) and Pure Car and Truck Carriers (PCTCs). The requirements focus on reducing the risk of an EV fire spreading beyond the space where it starts. A key hazard comes from lithium-ion batteries, where malfunction can result in thermal runaway and severe fires that can be difficult to control. Lithium-ion battery fires can also release toxic and corrosive gases, creating additional risks for people on board and the marine environment. Aerial image of electric vehicles As increasing numbers of electric vehicles are manufactured, shipped and transported by sea, LR’s new notation provides ship designers, shipyards and owners with dedicated requirements for incorporating EV fire safety measures into vessel design. Gabriele Sancin, Fire & Safety Team Lead – Specialist Vessels, LR, said: “Electric vehicles are an increasingly important part of the cargo carried by vehicle carriers and RoRo ships, but lithium-ion batteries present specific fire risks that need to be considered from the design stage. “FIRE (EV) gives designers, shipyards and owners clear requirements covering detection, structural protection, ventilation, suppression and firefighting arrangements. The objective is to ensure vessels are designed with effective measures to manage these risks and support the safe carriage of electric vehicles.” Electric vehicle signage FIRE (EV) applies specifically to ship design, including vehicle-space arrangements and the systems and equipment serving those spaces. Operational measures, including crew training requirements, fall outside the scope of the notation. The new notation is included in Chapter 6 of Part 6 of LR’s July 2026 Rules and Regulations for the Classification of Ships. Source: Lloyd’s Register 2026-11-18 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Europe’s Pitch Book: Spain – the comeback kid
articles.summary: Assuming you are mildly interested in Europe, you will have noticed Spain’s economic strength in recent years. GDP has been expanding at an annual 2.9% rate over the last three years, more than double the EU’s 1.1% pace. That strength makes Spain a natural candidate for this series, where we bring Europe’s countries...
articles.body: Europe’s Pitch Book: Spain – the comeback kid in World Economy News 18/11/2026 Assuming you are mildly interested in Europe, you will have noticed Spain’s economic strength in recent years. GDP has been expanding at an annual 2.9% rate over the last three years, more than double the EU’s 1.1% pace. That strength makes Spain a natural candidate for this series, where we bring Europe’s countries to life as different characters in the European family. The aim is to help you get to know them better and uncover qualities and potential that might otherwise go unnoticed. After Poland (the quiet overachiever), Romania (the gifted one) and Italy (the resilient Nonna), Spain is the ‘comeback kid’. For more than a decade, the country was a problem child, getting into trouble during the eurozone crisis and weighing on the region’s overall performance. Today, the picture is very different. So how did Spain pull off the turnaround, and how much further can it go? We look at the drivers behind its success and why we believe there is still plenty of room to outperform the European average. Step 1: Deflating a real estate bubble Spain ran into trouble during the financial crisis, but not so much because of its government finances. Its debt-to-GDP ratio was actually below 40%. The real problem was an unsustainable build-up of private-sector leverage, funded externally through a large current account deficit and used largely to fuel a real estate boom. Once that cycle turned, the effects hit the banks and eventually the government finances too. Fixing it required a major balance-sheet restructuring and a gradual unwinding of the property bubble. Much like in Italy, this slowed down economic growth. That restructuring has now largely come to an end, although private-sector loan growth has continued to lag nominal GDP growth. Private debt has roughly halved relative to GDP Consolidated debt of households and non-financial corporations as percentage of GDP Source: Eurostat Step 2: Getting people to work Spain is a rapidly ageing country. But over the last decade, it has still managed to add a lot of workers to its labour force. As in other European countries, this has come through higher participation among women and older workers. The pace of the increase has been somewhat stronger among women and somewhat weaker among older workers, compared to the rest of Europe. Participation rates for both groups remain below the European average, suggesting there is room for further gains. Far more women and older people in work, though still below the EU Source: Eurostat Spain used to stand out for its extremely high youth unemployment, which reached an alarming 55.5% in 2013. By September 2026, it had fallen to 22.8%. That is clearly a big improvement, but it also shows Spain has more room to catch up: the rate is still seven percentage points above the European average. Youth unemployment has more than halved Source: Eurostat Step 3: Migration Looking back over the past 25 years, however, participation has not been the main driver of Spain’s strong employment growth. Migration has played a much bigger role. Spain took a completely different stance on migration than most other European countries. It has been and continues to be especially open to people from Latin America, where the cultural and language barriers tend to be lower. Many of these migrants are now in employment and account for around 70% of Spain’s employment growth, suggesting that continued immigration could remain an important source of labour force and economic growth. Foreign-born workers are driving Spain’s employment growth Employment by place of birth Source: Eurostat Since 2015, the combined effect of higher participation and migration, partly offset by fewer hours worked per person, has increased total hours worked in Spain by almost 18%. That is roughly twice the European average. This has gone hand-in-hand with weaker growth in productivity per hour worked but, looking ahead, the good news is that labour participation still has room to rise and migration could continue, helping to significantly soften the impact of an ageing population. Step 4: Strong industrial clusters Spain is Europe’s second-largest car producer after Germany, and it is now attracting a new wave of investment from Chinese manufacturers looking for a production base inside the EU. Cars built locally avoid the EU tariffs imposed on electric vehicles imported from China. Chery has been producing cars with Spanish brand Ebro at the former Nissan plant in Barcelona since late 2024. Leapmotor is starting production at Stellantis’s plant near Zaragoza, while Geely agreed in July 2026 to build two electric models at Ford’s Valencia plant from 2028. MG, meanwhile, has chosen Galicia for its first EU factory. Battery manufacturers are following too, with CATL and Stellantis building a €4.1bn battery plant in Zaragoza. But Spain’s industrial strength goes beyond cars. Andalusia has developed an aerospace cluster around Seville and Cádiz, with roughly 150 companies generating turnover of €3.2bn in 2025, up 11%, and directly employing around 16,400 people. Seville hosts some of Airbus’s final assembly lines, while Cádiz specialises in components and advanced composites. Over the last ten years, industrial production picked up gradually, which means Spain outperformed France, Italy and especially Germany. Manufacturing accounted for 10.6% of GDP in 2025 while real value added grew by 2.2%, making it a strong contributor to Spain’s growth. Step 5: Broadening out from tourism to business services Tourism has long been an important part of Spain’s services sector. The sector was hit hard during Covid but has since recovered, with the net export surplus reaching 4.3% of GDP in 2025. Yet tourism has not been the fastest-growing part of Spain’s services sector. In recent years, Spain has emerged as a business services hub for European companies. Exports of business and professional services have more than tripled, from €14bn in 2013 to €47bn in 2025, with 57% going to other European countries. Foreign firms are also hiring in Spain: in 2024, they accounted for 43% of Spain’s IT services workforce, or around 216,000 jobs. The sector is one of the forces behind Spain’s large current account surplus, together with tourism and a declining deficit in goods trade. Looking ahead, we expect both tourism and professional services to grow at a faster pace than most other sectors. A large current account surplus on the back of services exports Net trade surplus or deficit as a percentage of GDP Source: Eurostat Step 6: Newfound talents But the real growth spurt has come from Spain’s strong push into renewables, playing to Spain’s natural strengths: plenty of space, sun, wind and hydro potential. Wind and solar now represent over 40% of power generation. And since 2022, this has paid off, with average electricity prices well below the European average, giving energy-intensive companies a competitive advantage. Spain’s green success, however, goes beyond using renewable technologies. The country also produces them, both for its domestic market and for export. It has a strong wind-power industry, with manufacturers like Siemens Gamesa, Windar and Haizea concentrated mainly in the north, including in the Basque Country. Spain is a pioneer in niche areas such as floating offshore wind and in addition provides components for the solar industry like solar trackers. Spain is also benefiting from the AI boom. It has seen a surge in exports of electrical power equipment (transformers and switchgear) and cooling equipment to the US. We see the same trend elsewhere in Europe too but since 2022, Spain’s exports have risen by 93% compared with a European average of 67%. Electrical power equipment recorded the largest increase in absolute terms, while data-centre cooling equipment saw the fastest growth, at 153%, compared with just 37% for the EU27. This gives Spain two sources of future growth. Its competitive electricity prices make it an attractive location for energy-intensive sectors, from industry to data centres, while its strength in producing green technologies offers further industrial potential. Both are areas with significant room to grow. Sun and wind are growing, lowering electricity costs for firms Source: Eurostat Step 7: Spain has options to raise its growth potential Given the much stronger increase in hours worked, it should not come as a surprise that productivity growth has been slower in Spain than elsewhere in Europe. Currently, Spain’s productivity level is about 5% below the EU average, and well below that of other Western European countries. We have written before that Spain will need to boost productivity growth if it is to remain one of Europe’s growth frontrunners. Productivity growth has lagged the rest of the EU since 2015 Source: Eurostat In the short term, this does not seem particularly urgent. Spain has beaten our growth forecast once again this year, expanding by 2.6%. For the next two years, we expect growth of about 2%. That is still well above the eurozone average, but the growth differential is strongly driven by the continued inflow of workers. In the longer term, in addition to labour participation and migration, we see two related ways to increase the country’s growth potential further. Firstly, the country has a very low share of R&D investment and low levels of investment in ICT. Sectors producing ICT goods and services account for a small part of the economy, while more traditional sectors such as construction, trade and transport are relatively large. These sectors are characterised by many small firms, and consolidation could lead to significant efficiency gains. With good broadband and decent digital skills, Spain’s problem is less about access to technology and more about its diffusion across the economy, the ability of firms to scale up and the country’s sectoral composition. One solution would be to make taxes and regulation less dependent on company size. A second option would be to make the labour market less rigid and more flexible. Current labour laws often make it unattractive for companies to scale up or down in response to demand. As a workaround, companies have relied on temporary employment contracts. Recent reforms have reduced their use, but Spain still has relatively strong protections for established workers, and high turnover and insecurity for workers at the margin. The latter makes investment in training less attractive, both for workers and their employers. The country also lacks active labour market policies to help workers move between jobs and sectors. Further labour market reforms could help Spain catch up with Europe’s productivity frontier. So, looking at the supply side of the economy, both on the corporate and labour market side, Spain still has the ingredients at hand to boost future productivity growth. Two brakes on productivity: little business R&D and many jobs in low-productivity services Source: Eurostat Step 8: Awaken domestic demand A final potential source of support for the economy could come from Spain’s demand side. As in many other European countries, households are saving a larger share of their income. In Spain, this follows decades of deleveraging, with the household savings rate recently around two percentage points above pre-Covid levels. Three types of measures could put those savings to greater use: reducing the need for precautionary saving, for example by improving job security; redistributing income towards households with a lower income as they have a higher propensity to consume; and creating stronger incentives to invest savings, either through financial markets or directly in the real economy. As with the supply side, the choices are political, but there clearly is upside potential here too. Spanish consumers are putting more money aside Financial savings as percentage of disposable income Source: Eurostat An impressive job, but much more to do Spain has been on an impressive journey. The former problem child deserves its new status as the comeback kid: deflating a real estate bubble, revamping its labour supply, strengthening its manufacturing sector, jumping into business services and discovering a talent for green technology – consider it all done. Comeback kids tend to be ambitious, and having tasted success, Spain may be no different. It still has more to gain, from exploiting its competitive advantage in energy to further expanding its labour force and catching up with Europe’s productivity frontier. If its ambition continues, Spain has plenty of scope to keep outpacing the eurozone average. The European family will likely be watching with a mix of admiration and envy. U.S. Coast Guard Photo The U.S. Coast Guard’s newest polar icebreaker, Storis (WAGB 21), has returned to Seattle following a 133-day Arctic deployment that included monitoring Chinese research vessels, conducting fisheries enforcement operations and testing military capabilities in ice-covered waters. The 360-foot cutter returned to its temporary homeport on Saturday, November 14, after traveling more than 17,000 nautical miles through the Arctic Ocean and waters around Alaska. According to the Coast Guard, Storis served as the sole U.S. surface asset in the High Arctic during portions of its deployment, supporting maritime security, border enforcement and sovereignty missions. Under Operation Frontier Sentinel, the cutter spent more than 300 hours monitoring foreign-flagged research vessels, including four Chinese-flagged ships operating over the U.S. extended continental shelf. The patrol also marked the first designated law enforcement mission conducted by a U.S. polar icebreaker in more than 20 years. The crew inspected fishing vessels in the Bering Sea, including a joint boarding and fisheries processing plant inspection with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Office of Law Enforcement. In another milestone, Storis conducted what the Coast Guard described as the first live-fire gunnery exercise by one of its surface vessels operating in ice-covered Arctic waters in decades. The exercise was intended to assess weapons employment in extreme conditions and generate data to guide future Arctic operations. The cutter also conducted a simulated replenishment-at-sea exercise with Coast Guard Cutter Stratton near Unalaska, Alaska. Crews used Storis’ dynamic positioning system and onboard sensors to demonstrate close-quarters maneuvering capabilities needed for replenishment operations in remote waters. During Operation Tundra Merlin, Storis operated alongside Coast Guard cutters Munro and Fir and the Royal Canadian Navy’s HMCS Max Bernays, strengthening coordination between U.S. and Canadian forces. The cutter also assisted the grounded fishing vessel Aleutian Dream, providing initial assistance and escorting the vessel back to Dutch Harbor. “We are serving in a moment of great change in our service, nation and world,” said Capt. Corey Kerns, commanding officer of Storis. He said the crew’s efforts had transformed the vessel into an operational, multi-mission military asset. The deployment included testing unmanned aircraft in extreme cold alongside the Coast Guard Research and Development Center and the Defense Innovation Unit. Five sorties totaling nine flight hours evaluated drone performance in high-latitude conditions, supporting the Icebreaker Collaboration Effort between the United States, Canada and Finland. Storis, formerly the commercial icebreaking vessel Aiviq, was acquired by the Coast Guard in December 2024 and commissioned in August 2025, becoming the service’s first new polar icebreaker in more than two decades. The deployment comes as the Coast Guard’s already limited polar icebreaking fleet faces continued strain. The service’s medium icebreaker Healy has been sidelined since suffering a major engineering casualty in July, forcing the cancellation of its planned 2026 Arctic mission. The situation underscores Washington’s continuing struggle to maintain polar capabilities as competition with Russia and China intensifies. REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo By Arsalan Shahla and Jen Judson (Bloomberg) — American warplanes hit an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Persian Gulf on Tuesday, a US military official said, as the two sides intensified tit-for-tat attacks in the ongoing war. The strike on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps site was in response to Iranian aggression targeting US personnel and assets, the official said, declining to be named. Earlier on Tuesday, Iran’s semi-official Mehr News Agency reported that US forces had struck several locations on Qeshm Island, adding the assault caused no casualties or damage to critical and public-service infrastructure. The US bombing came after the third Iranian attack on Bahrain in less than a week. President Donald Trump separately said the US is investigating a report about potential Iranian plans to target Washington. The flurry of recent incidents — as well as increased Iranian attacks on commercial vessels — suggests an intensification of the low-grade clashes that have persisted throughout the ongoing stalemate between the US and Iran. “For both the US and Iran, there’s an operational rationale for their strikes, from reducing threats to their ability to operate in the Strait of Hormuz,” said Becca Wasser, defense lead for Bloomberg Economics. “But we’ve seen throughout this conflict the mismatch between operational objectives and political realities, where tit-for-tat strikes quickly escalate.” Neither side has shown a willingness to compromise on an issue that might pave the way to a resolution, such as the lifting of a US naval blockade or concessions from Iran on its nuclear program. Qatar, the main mediator between Washington and Tehran, was due to meet with representatives of the Islamic Republic on Tuesday, part of a long-running effort to find a diplomatic off-ramp. Oil prices gained amid the fresh flareups, having plunged following the Republican defeat in the US midterm elections earlier this month. Brent crude rose toward $94 a barrel, still up more than 50% for the year. Qeshm lies off Iran’s southern coast near the Strait of Hormuz — the critical transit point for oil and gas that’s long been the focal point of the conflict. The US launched limited attacks on the island earlier this month, saying they were defensive in nature and designed to help energy tankers and other vessels get through the strait safely. Earlier Tuesday, Iran’s parliamentary speaker and lead negotiator with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, warned that Tehran would retaliate against civilian infrastructure near US and Israeli bases if Washington did the same. His comments, a standard Iranian response to any perceived indication of US escalation, followed a New York Times report that water infrastructure sites in Iran “may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup.” This amounted to “prepping the next round on civilian” infrastructure, Ghalibaf said. “We’ll apply your logic consistently and even-handedly.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: HJSC operating profit surges as container shipbuilding drives growth
articles.summary: HJ Shipbuilding & Construction (HJSC) reported a sharp increase in earnings for the first nine months of 2026, supported by stronger performance in its shipbuilding division and continued construction of high-value container vessels. The South Korean company recorded consolidated revenue of KRW 2.0044 trillion, up...
articles.body: HJ Shipbuilding & Construction (HJSC) reported a sharp increase in earnings for the first nine months of 2026, supported by stronger performance in its shipbuilding division and continued construction of high-value container vessels. The South Korean company recorded consolidated revenue of KRW 2.0044 trillion, up 46.3% from KRW 1.3701 trillion in the same period last year. Operating profit increased to KRW 155.4 billion from KRW 16.6 billion, while net income reached KRW 130.6 billion, compared with KRW 2.9 billion a year earlier. The results, disclosed in a regulatory filing on 12 November, extend the improvement recorded during the first half of 2026. Container shipbuilding supports stronger profitability HJSC attributed much of its earnings growth to improved profitability in its shipbuilding division, which includes commercial and special-purpose vessels. Construction of environmentally friendly, high-value container ships gained momentum during the reporting period, contributing to higher revenue and stronger margins. The shipbuilding division generated revenue of KRW 1.1297 trillion, an increase of 88.1% from KRW 600.5 billion in the first nine months of 2025. Its operating profit reached KRW 149.7 billion, accounting for most of the group’s total operating earnings. Special-purpose ship projects, including maintenance, repair and overhaul work for the US Navy, also supported the division’s financial performance. According to HJSC, increased dock utilisation and improvements in production efficiency helped maintain operations despite fewer working days during the summer and Chuseok holiday periods. Meanwhile, the construction division reported revenue of KRW 874.2 billion and operating profit of KRW 5.6 billion. The division continued to benefit from public-sector construction, civil engineering and housing projects. “The increased share of revenue from high-value-added vessels and various special-purpose ship projects in the shipbuilding division, along with stable order wins and business operations in the construction division, contributed to our strong performance,” said an HJSC official. Looking ahead, HJSC plans to maintain its focus on profitability across both divisions. The company intends to improve its competitiveness in shipbuilding while pursuing selective construction contracts and tighter project cost management.
