articles.title: Vestas CEO Calls For EU Crackdown on Chinese Software Used in Wind Sector
articles.summary: As the European Union weighs tougher cybersecurity rules, it should consider a ban on Chinese components and technology containing software in critical energy infrastructure, the CEO of Danish wind turbine maker Vestas told Reuters."When it comes to critical infrastructure…
articles.body: Vestas CEO Calls For EU Crackdown on Chinese Software Used in Wind Sector Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 17, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Peter Adams As the European Union weighs tougher cybersecurity rules, it should consider a ban on Chinese components and technology containing software in critical energy infrastructure, the CEO of Danish wind turbine maker Vestas told Reuters. "When it comes to critical infrastructure, meaning technology or components that has a software element in it, I think we should have a very upfront 'no thank you'," CEO Henrik Andersen said when asked whether Europe should adopt rules similar to China’s restrictions on foreign technology. "The energy assets you build now last 30 to 50 years, and you have to make sure you can control them yourself," he said. The European Union is revising its cybersecurity rules and requirements for European-made equipment while governments expand their power grids to handle increased renewable energy supply. China's commerce ministry has said it would take strong countermeasures if the bloc adopts the revised Cybersecurity Act proposed in January, arguing the law would abandon technological neutrality and undermine China-EU trade. Chinese manufacturers supplied a fraction of Europe's new turbines last year but are pushing to enter the market. Vestas' Andersen said the EU should require that about half of its wind assets are made in Europe, and that a turbine’s control systems and software should be treated separately from that requirement. A German developer dropped China's Ming Yang from a North Sea project last year. Britain said in March it would not support the use of turbines from China's Ming Yang in UK offshore wind on security grounds. Ming Yang in a statement to Reuters on Monday said it stores all turbine data locally in Europe, that operators retain full control, and that no remote access is permitted without the operator's explicit approval. CHINA HAS ALSO TIGHTENED RULES Andersen noted that Chinese authorities have imposed similar rules, telling Vestas that it could no longer monitor the sensors on its own turbines or update its turbines' software remotely from Europe, on the grounds that foreign access posed a risk to China's grid. "China put a marker in the sand five years ago, and now it's time that we say that marker counts on both sides," Andersen told Reuters at the company's headquarters in Copenhagen. Chinese utilities are replacing Western equipment with domestic alternatives, Poland's state-funded Centre for Eastern Studies said in a report last month. Andersen, whose company stands to gain if Chinese rivals are kept out of Europe, said he did not support a blanket ban on Chinese components but that if Europe believed in free competition, Vestas should have the same access to China's market, which it no longer has. "If we are going to play football, then let's play football. Eleven a side and a referee in the middle," he said. He said attacks that cranked up fridge temperatures at supermarkets across Europe this month were a reminder that whoever holds the software updates controls the machine, whether it is a refrigerator, car or wind turbine. While no one has claimed responsibility for those attacks, they have heightened concerns among European authorities about hybrid threats to infrastructure. "There is a security risk if you are not the one holding the username, password and access," Andersen said. Ming Yang in the written statement said it also supported cybersecurity rules being applied equally to every supplier, but added that supplier-specific assessment and verifiable safeguards were preferable to "blanket exclusions based on country of origin". The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU and China’s commerce ministry did not respond to requests for comment. (Reuters)

articles.summary: The number of empty tankers sailing to collect cargoes of Middle East crude is sliding, a trend that could jeopardize the recent revival in the region’s oil flows to global markets, according to Tankertrackers.com, a firm that monitors vessel movements.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Faraways/Shutterstock By Alaric Nightingale (Bloomberg) — The number of empty tankers sailing to collect cargoes of Middle East crude is sliding, a trend that could jeopardize the recent revival in the region’s oil flows to global markets, according to Tankertrackers.com, a firm that monitors vessel movements. The industry uses two main ship types to get oil from the Persian Gulf to the world: very large crude carriers, which transport 2 million-barrel cargoes, and Suezmaxes that move about half that. The collective capacity of those vessels sailing empty to the region has declined by about 40% since the end of August, according to Tankertrackers.com figures. While the market is intensely focused on how much oil leaves the Middle East, those flows are only possible if there’s a steady stream of ships arriving to pick up the barrels. The Iran war has meant that some vessels refuse to go through the Strait of Hormuz, instead receiving cargoes in locations like the Gulf of Oman from tankers that are willing to risk shuttling through the crucial waterway. There are “not enough vacant tankers to take oil out of the region,” Tankertrackers.com’s co-founder, Samir Madani, said by WhatsApp. “It’s one thing to bring the oil out into the Gulf of Oman via the Strait of Hormuz, but it seems like there isn’t enough to take the oil out of the Gulf of Oman.” In broad terms, there has been a dip in flows from the region at large so far this month, though it’s still unclear what the causes of the drop are, the exact scale of the decrease, or how long-lasting the decline will be, Madani said. For now, though, the number of ships transferring cargoes onto other ships outside the Persian Gulf remains high, enabling shipments toward customers to continue for the time being, he said. Oil tanker rates have declined from record levels over the past few weeks, helping to reduce the cost of delivering crude to customers. Any shortage in the number of empty vessels would support rates. Iran has attacked shipping consistently throughout the conflict, something that has deterred transits. The number of incidents reported officially jumped last month, and remains at high levels so far in November, according to data from the International Maritime Organization and the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: Nearly three decades before a tanker slammed into a docked river cruise ship in New Orleans, the National Transportation Safety Board warned that passenger vessels along the Mississippi River waterfront...

The accident prompted NTSB safety recommendations addressing the risks posed by large commercial vessels to passenger ships docked along the Mississippi River. (Image: NTSB accident investigation report) Nearly three decades before a tanker slammed into a docked river cruise ship in New Orleans, the National Transportation Safety Board warned that passenger vessels along the Mississippi River waterfront were vulnerable to being struck by large commercial ships and urged authorities to consider relocating them or installing protective measures. The warning came in a 1998 NTSB investigation into the Bright Field accident, when a Liberian-flagged bulk carrier lost propulsion and crashed into the New Orleans riverfront, injuring 62 people. Now, the findings are drawing renewed attention following Friday’s allision between the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Atlantic Asphalt and American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage , which capsized after being struck while docked near the Crescent City Connection Bridge right in the heart of downtown New Orleans. All 190 passengers and crew aboard the riverboat survived the November 13 accident, although 32 people were taken to hospitals. The similarities between the two accidents are striking, particularly because the earlier investigation specifically identified the dangers facing passenger vessels moored along the busy commercial waterway. In its report on the December 14, 1996, Bright Field accident, the NTSB concluded that the Coast Guard, Port of New Orleans and waterfront operators had failed to adequately assess, manage or mitigate the risks of locating unprotected commercial facilities in areas vulnerable to vessel strikes. Notably, the Bright Field stopped just 70 feet from the docked gaming vessel Queen of New Orleans , while its bow wave caused the gangway of the nearby paddlewheeler Creole Queen to collapse, sending three passengers into the Mississippi River. The Creole Queen had 190 passengers and crew aboard — the same approximate number reported aboard American Heritage during Friday’s collision. The NTSB subsequently criticized the vessels’ emergency evacuation arrangements and issued additional safety recommendations. In its report, the agency issued two recommendations addressing the placement of passenger vessels along the river. Recommendation M-98-1 directed the Coast Guard, working with the Port of New Orleans, to reassess the risks of passenger vessel berths along the Mississippi River’s left descending bank and determine whether vessels should be moved to safer locations or protected through procedural, operational or physical barriers. Another recommendation, M-98-10, directed the Port of New Orleans to undertake the same assessment in cooperation with the Coast Guard. The NTSB also called for a comprehensive risk assessment of maritime and shoreside activities throughout the port, including measures to reduce the dangers associated with commercial vessel traffic. In that earlier investigation, the NTSB highlighted the risks created by large vessels navigating the narrow, heavily trafficked river near passenger terminals, commercial developments and other vulnerable infrastructure, and identified potential mitigation measures including reduced vessel speeds, tug escorts and moving passenger vessels to safer locations. The danger of mechanical failure was also well documented. When the Coast Guard subsequently finalized additional Lower Mississippi River navigation regulations in 1999, it noted that more than 300 self-propelled vessels of at least 1,600 gross tons had experienced propulsion losses, steering casualties or engine irregularities on the Mississippi River during 1995 and 1996. The 1999 regulations established additional operating requirements for larger commercial vessels and required certain passenger vessels moored or anchored in the river to maintain manned pilothouse watches and monitor emergency communications. Those requirements, now contained in 33 CFR 165.810 , were intended to improve navigation safety and allow passenger vessel crews to respond quickly to emergencies. The regulatory action demonstrates that authorities did respond to the earlier accident. However, the extent to which the NTSB’s separate recommendations concerning passenger vessel placement and protective barriers were implemented at individual berths remains unclear. The current official disposition of recommendations M-98-1 and M-98-10 has not been independently confirmed. Nor has it been established what specific risk assessments or protective measures were in place at the berth occupied by American Heritage . Those questions could become significant as investigators examine the circumstances surrounding Friday’s collision. According to the NTSB’s ongoing investigation , the Atlantic Asphalt was traveling upriver near the Crescent City Connection Bridge when it experienced what investigators described as a steering casualty. Preliminary information recovered from the tanker’s voyage data recorder indicates the vessel’s rudder remained in a starboard position, causing the tanker to veer toward the river’s east bank. Approximately two minutes later, the tanker struck American Heritage at its berth. The riverboat subsequently overturned, forcing passengers and crew to evacuate as emergency responders and nearby commercial vessels rushed to assist. Investigators have not determined what caused the steering failure. While the Bright Field accident involved a loss of propulsion rather than steering, both incidents demonstrate the consequences of a large commercial vessel losing maneuvering capability in the confined waters of downtown New Orleans. The NTSB has not determined whether the location of the American Heritage berth or the protective measures in place contributed to Friday’s accident. Nor is there evidence at this stage that either vessel or port authorities violated the regulations adopted following the earlier casualty. But the 1998 recommendations raise an important question nearly 30 years after federal investigators identified the danger of large commercial ships striking passenger vessels along the New Orleans waterfront. For the NTSB, which has repeatedly warned across transportation sectors about the dangers of leaving identified safety risks unresolved, the latest collision presents another opportunity to examine whether lessons from an earlier accident could have made a difference in this latest case. articles.title: Port of NY/NJ approves planning for heating and refrigeration plant at Newark airport
articles.summary: The Board of Commissioners of the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey has approved a request to advance plans to replace the central heating and refrigeration plant serving Terminals A, B and C at Newark Liberty International Airport. The work may include planning for phased construction at operating facilities...
articles.body: The Board of Commissioners of the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey has approved a request to advance plans to replace the central heating and refrigeration plant serving Terminals A, B and C at Newark Liberty International Airport. The work may include planning for phased construction at operating facilities and other projects, together with expenses linked to procuring construction awards. The new plant is intended to be a foundational part of the airport’s modernisation, supplying heating, cooling and potentially power to more than 5 million square feet of existing and future terminal space. The existing plant was built in 1973 and is nearing the end of its useful life. Its current site cannot house the larger facility needed to serve the new and expanded terminals envisaged in the EWR Vision Plan, and the Port Authority’s 2026-2035 Capital Plan includes funds for its replacement. The project is expected to be delivered in phases while maintaining passenger service in all terminals, and to include sustainability measures aligned with the agency’s net-zero roadmap. Alongside the Board’s decision, the Port Authority issued a nonbinding Request for Expressions of Interest to identify firms interested in the future procurement and to gather market feedback on commercial structure, technical delivery, phasing, performance management, decarbonisation and future-proofing. It is particularly seeking responses from infrastructure equity investors, developers, energy-as-a-service providers, operators, financial institutions, designers and builders with experience of complex energy and aviation infrastructure. A competitive, transparent procurement is intended to follow. Under the proposed framework, the selected developer would design, build, finance, operate and maintain the plant and its distribution infrastructure, and would work with, and potentially contract with, airport energy users including terminal operators, airlines and other tenants. The plant forms part of the wider transformation of Newark Liberty that began with the opening of Terminal A in 2023, which won the 2024 World’s Best New Airport Terminal award and a five-star Skytrax rating. A new AirTrain Newark is under construction, planning and design are under way for a new Terminal B, and a new entry point to the airport’s rail station is being built to improve access to NJ TRANSIT and Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor services. Chairman Kevin O’Toole said the investments so far have begun a generational transformation of the airport. Executive Director Kathryn Garcia said the request for expressions of interest helps turn the EWR Vision Plan into reality and is an invitation to invest not only in Newark Airport but in New Jersey itself.

November 17, 2026 © Adobe Stock/DedMityay A liquefied petroleum gas tanker sank off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast on Tuesday, Bulgaria's defence ministry said, a few dozen miles from where another ship went down after a drone attack a day earlier. The Liberian-flagged vessel, Gas Husky, sent a distress signal before sinking approximately 50 miles east of Byala, the ministry said. The Transport Ministry said that all 19 crew members had been evacuated from the life raft to an air base in the town of Varna. It said that the tanker was carrying 3,400 metric tons of liquefied petroleum gas at the time it sank. The vessel's Greece-based manager did not respond immediately to a request for comment. The cause of the incident, which occurred inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, and the state of the tanker and the crew were not immediately clear. Mario Smarkov, Varna regional governor said there had been no pollution recorded in the area. On Monday a cargo ship carrying wheat sank about 40 nautical miles off the same stretch of coast after it was attacked by at least one drone. That was the latest in a spate of attacks that have left more than 20 seafarers missing and feared dead, raising concerns about the widening conflict between Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea. "The motor vessel GAS HUSKY disappeared from radar shortly after midnight, and at 0802 (0602 GMT) this morning, its emergency beacon — which signals that a vessel has sunk — was activated," the defence ministry said. At least 17 vessels have been attacked off the coast of Bulgaria and Romania since mid-July, according to maritime security firm Diaplous. The waters off the shores of the two NATO countries have become the primary route for shipments from Ukraine, one of the world's biggest grain exporters, the Black Sea ports of which have come under constant fire from Russia since its invasion. articles.title: US Military Radar System in Bahrain Attacked by Iran
articles.summary: Iran fired drones at a US military radar system in Bahrain on Tuesday and the crew of a tanker was reported missing in the Strait of Hormuz, despite talks between Iran and mediators Oman and Qatar.Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said…
articles.body: US Military Radar System in Bahrain Attacked by Iran Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 17, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Zerophoto Iran fired drones at a US military radar system in Bahrain on Tuesday and the crew of a tanker was reported missing in the Strait of Hormuz, despite talks between Iran and mediators Oman and Qatar. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said the radar system at Bahrain's Sheikh Isa base had been targeted, and warned Bahrain over its alliance with the US and stance towards Shi'ite clergy. Bahrain, which is home to the headquarters of the US Fifth Fleet, said it had intercepted the attack and there were no reports of casualties or damage. Later on Tuesday, Iranian media reported an explosion on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, and cited an Iranian official as saying the US had carried out an attack there without causing damage to infrastructure. Asked for comment, the US military's Central Command said it had no updates. Washington carried out limited strikes on Qeshm earlier this month. Qatari and Iranian officials were meeting on Tuesday, Qatar said, as part of efforts to mediate an end to nearly nine months of war that has destabilised the Middle East and pushed up global energy prices. The talks are aimed at "bridging perspectives and narrowing the gap between proposals presented on the ground," Qatari spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said. They coincide with a visit to Oman by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi. Oman's Foreign Ministry said he discussed safeguarding maritime corridors and ensuring the smooth flow of global shipping and trade, as well as preventing military escalation, with Oman's foreign minister. Oman and Iran lie on opposite sides of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that carried about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies before the war but is now partly blocked by Iran. Oman has previously held talks with Tehran about controlling traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Araqchi said in a post on Telegram that he also met Oman's Sultan Haitham ‌bin Tariq and informed him about Iran's diplomatic initiative to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. RISE IN ATTACKS ON TANKERS The war has ground to a stalemate, with US President Donald Trump saying he might hold off from attacking Iran if the US does not face what he described as provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthi group in Yemen. Trump said on Tuesday the US was taking seriously the possibility that Iran could be ‌planning an attack involving a so-called dirty bomb in Washington, after being asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments. Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson said the report was part of a US campaign "to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs" using "baseless allegations". Trump has also said he will maintain a US naval blockade on Iran because it has continued to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, which is a sticking point in negotiations. Attacks on tankers have increased this month in the strait, and the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the crew of a tanker passing through the waterway was unaccounted for after being attacked north of ⁠the Omani port city of Khasab. Iran's Revolutionary Guards and navy said on Tuesday that a ship carrying LNG and two oil tankers had caught fire in the strait. Reuters could not independently verify the reports. Benchmark Brent crude futures were up 0.4% at $92.76 a barrel on Tuesday, much higher than before the war but well below April's wartime peak of $126.41. IRANIAN WARNING The war also continues to spill over into other parts of the Middle East as Iran puts pressure on Washington through its Houthi allies, who have carried out attacks on Saudi Arabia and seized areas along the Yemeni coast on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, hoping to squeeze Gulf oil producers. Tuesday's attack on Bahrain, a Shi'ite-majority country ruled by a Sunni Muslim family, followed the sentencing there of 64 people, mostly Shi'ite clerics, to life in prison on charges of colluding with Iran to undermine the state. Iran's foreign ministry condemned the court's ruling on Tuesday and said the accusations were baseless. Tehran has long denied interference in Bahrain's internal affairs. Iran also fired on Bahrain two days ago,saying it had targeted a US radar system at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base following what it said were hostile US actions. Iran's Revolutionary Guards spokesperson said Bahrain had made "three key mistakes", which he listed as "cooperating in the invasion of the Islamic Republic of Iran, remaining within the US security bubble, and encroaching on the sanctity of Shi'ite religious authority". These, "if continued, will jeopardize its survival in the region's new security order," ⁠Hossein Mohebbi said. (Reuters)

articles.summary: Norway is moving a step closer to testing nuclear propulsion for commercial ships, with a consortium including shipbuilder VARD and offshore vessel operator Island Offshore securing NOK 20 million ($2...

VARD/Island Offshore Norway is moving a step closer to testing nuclear propulsion for commercial ships, with a consortium including shipbuilder VARD and offshore vessel operator Island Offshore securing NOK 20 million ($2 million) in government funding to develop an integrated nuclear power system for offshore vessels. The Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) project , led by Emerald Nuclear Norway, aims to move the technology from engineering studies into full-scale testing, with a first vessel deployment targeted for 2031 or 2032. The initial funding comes from the Research Council of Norway and supports a broader development program that will bring together reactor technology, ship design, electrical systems and vessel operations. The first phase, scheduled for 2027, will establish a test facility at Stette, near Ålesund, where the partners plan to assemble and test a full-scale representation of the proposed shipboard propulsion system. Importantly, the initial testing will not involve an operating nuclear reactor. Instead, the system will use electric heating to simulate the reactor’s thermal output, allowing engineers to evaluate how the propulsion and power systems work together before moving to nuclear operation. Testing will examine normal vessel operations, rapid changes in power demand, system performance, stress conditions and crew interaction. The project is based on Emerald Nuclear’s 5-megawatt-electric GEM Microreactor technology, using a gas-cooled reactor design coupled with a supercritical carbon dioxide turbine system to generate electricity. The integrated system will also include energy storage, remote monitoring, power management and shipboard automation. According to Emerald Nuclear , the first phase has an estimated total cost of NOK 150 million ($15.6 million), with project partners providing substantial funding beyond the government grant. For VARD, part of Italy’s Fincantieri Group, the project represents another step toward bringing advanced nuclear technology into commercial shipbuilding. Its subsidiary Vard Electro will focus on integrating the power system with the electrical controls and automation systems used aboard ships. “We also view this funding award as a vital sign of national support for nuclear applications in maritime going forward,” said Håvard Vollset Lien, Vice President of Research and Innovation at Vard Group. Island Offshore, meanwhile, hopes to become the first offshore service vessel operator to install the system. “Nuclear energy has the potential to provide a new route to decarbonising offshore vessels without compromising the power, endurance and operational flexibility these ships require,” said Tommy Walaunet, CEO of Island Offshore. Emerald Nuclear is also proposing a different commercial model for shipboard nuclear power. Rather than requiring shipowners to purchase and operate reactors themselves, the company would retain ownership and operational responsibility, including maintenance and nuclear fuel management. Shipowners would instead pay for the electricity they use. The consortium also includes the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Imperial College London and engineering specialist Maskindynamikk, bringing together expertise in nuclear modelling, structural integrity, monitoring and marine operations. The project builds on Norway’s earlier NuProShip research initiatives, which have examined the feasibility of nuclear propulsion for commercial shipping. While significant technical testing, safety validation and regulatory work remain before the technology can be deployed at sea, the next phase will provide an early full-scale demonstration of how a nuclear energy system could be integrated into an offshore vessel. articles.body: The Port of Oakland and Everport Terminal Services, marked the arrival of new electric cargo-handling equipment at the Oakland Seaport. Everport has invested in eight battery-electric top picks, heavy-duty machines that stack containers weighing up to 100,000 pounds and load them onto trucks, a role historically filled by diesel equipment. The machines are American-made Taylor Machine Works ZLC996 electric container handlers, each expected to run two full shifts on a single charge. ETS funded the purchase privately. The arrival follows another step in October, when the port began construction of infrastructure improvements to convert the Matson Terminal to 100 percent zero-emissions operations. That work is part of a US$ 119 million investment from the Port and Freight Infrastructure Program, funded by the California State Transportation Agency. Together, the projects support the port’s goals of greater competitiveness, improved freight efficiency and lower emissions, in line with California’s wider clean transportation objectives. Ron Neal, President of Everport Terminal Services, said the company is committed to an efficient and sustainable operation, and called the investment an important step toward zero-emission cargo handling and modernising the terminal for the next generation. Port of Oakland Executive Director Kristi McKenney described the milestone as part of a journey toward zero emissions begun many years ago with many partners, and said the mix of public and private investment in US-made electric equipment creates jobs at the port and in towns across the country.

(Photo: Hanwha Defense USA) South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace and its U.S. subsidiary have successfully test-fired a Chunmoo guided missile from a vessel off the Mississippi coast, marking another step toward deploying precision-strike weapons aboard crewed and unmanned naval vessels. The launch took place Sunday, November 15, aboard a test-range vessel operated by Mississippi-based The Spaceport Company , using a palletized launcher designed to be installed on maritime platforms. According to Hanwha Defense USA, the firing completed a two-launch test campaign aimed at validating the Chunmoo missile system for operations at sea. The tests also evaluated the launcher and its electronics as the company works to develop a maritime strike capability that could be deployed across different classes of vessels. The effort comes as the U.S. Navy looks to expand its use of distributed maritime strike systems, including weapons carried aboard smaller warships and unmanned surface vessels. “Hanwha is answering the U.S. Navy’s call to produce and field modern strike capabilities from a maritime platform,” said Kevin Schoonover, executive vice president for missiles at Hanwha Defense USA. “By pairing Hanwha’s flagship Chunmoo missile and its palletized platform with next generation crewed and uncrewed vessels, we can deliver capabilities for the Navy at scale and a fraction of the cost of other systems.” Schoonover said data collected during the tests would help guide future development of palletized and containerized launch systems for distributed maritime operations and expeditionary strike missions. Unlike permanently installed missile launchers, palletized and containerized systems are designed to provide greater flexibility in how weapons are integrated aboard ships, potentially allowing a wider range of vessels to carry precision-strike capabilities. The demonstration also involved Magnet Defense, which deployed its research vessel to track and evaluate the missile launch. Hanwha Defense USA and Magnet Defense announced a strategic partnership in April to develop and produce medium unmanned surface vessels for the U.S. military. The partnership includes plans for a 38-meter unmanned vessel and the integration of advanced weapons and autonomous systems. The latest missile test could help advance those efforts, although Hanwha has not announced a timetable for operational deployment of the ship-based Chunmoo system. The Spaceport Company, which specializes in offshore launch operations, has conducted more than 10 launches using mobile launch vessels, barges and semi-submersible platforms. Hanwha said its testing program will continue to gather technical and operational data to support the development of maritime strike capabilities for future naval and expeditionary operations. articles.title: Study: Connecting Great Lakes, Inland Waterways Could Deliver Millions in Freight Savings
articles.summary: A new study commissioned by the American Great Lakes Ports Association (AGLPA) identifies opportunities to expand freight movements between the Great Lakes and U.S. inland waterways, potentially delivering millions of dollars in transportation…
articles.body: Study: Connecting Great Lakes, Inland Waterways Could Deliver Millions in Freight Savings Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 17, 2026 Copyright Reimar/AdobeStock A new study commissioned by the American Great Lakes Ports Association (AGLPA) identifies opportunities to expand freight movements between the Great Lakes and U.S. inland waterways, potentially delivering millions of dollars in transportation savings while improving supply chain flexibility and making better use of existing maritime infrastructure. Released November 17, The Great Freight Connection, prepared by transportation consultancy CPCS Transcom Inc., examines existing freight movements between the two systems and evaluates four potential trade corridors involving Port Milwaukee, Ports of Indiana–Burns Harbor and the Illinois International Port District. The findings reveal a significant disconnect between two of America's most important freight networks. In 2023, more than 138 million tons of cargo moved on the Great Lakes and Illinois Waterway systems, yet less than 1% of outbound Great Lakes tonnage moved to the Illinois Waterway. Conversely, approximately 5% of outbound Illinois Waterway cargo moved toward the Great Lakes. Despite their physical connection through Chicago, the systems largely function as separate freight networks. Putting Numbers to the Opportunity The study evaluates four representative trade lanes: grain shipments from Milwaukee to the Gulf Coast, steel from Burns Harbor to Peoria and St. Louis, liquid bulk from Joliet to Milwaukee, and salt moving north from the Gulf to Chicago. Among the most promising opportunities is steel transportation from Burns Harbor to inland markets. The study estimates potential savings of approximately $20.70 per ton for shipments to Peoria and $34.40 per ton to St. Louis compared with trucking. At an illustrative annual volume of 100,000 tons, those savings could reach approximately $2.07 million and $3.44 million, respectively. Moving that volume by water could also eliminate approximately 5,100 truck trips and reduce associated carbon emissions by roughly 87%. Other potential savings include $4.50 per ton for grain shipments, $1.80 for liquid bulk and $19.10 for salt. The figures represent modeled transportation savings rather than guaranteed commercial returns. “Northwest Indiana is home to some of the nation's largest steel producers, and giving them more ways to reach their customers is critical to their success,” said Ryan McCoy, Ports of Indiana–Burns Harbor Port Director. Infrastructure and Commercial Challenges The report identifies several obstacles to expanded cross-system shipping, including limited shipper awareness, established truck and rail relationships, bridge clearance restrictions, aging locks, seasonal navigation constraints and availability of suitable barges. A BNSF railroad bridge near Lemont, Illinois, was identified as a particular operational bottleneck, while lock closures and restrictions on barge movements can undermine service reliability. The study recommends 15 actions covering market development, industry partnerships, regulatory coordination and infrastructure improvements, including expanding lake-capable barge capacity and improving terminal information available to shippers. “By better connecting these systems, we can expand reliable and cost-effective transportation options, strengthen domestic commerce, and create growth opportunities for American industry and workers across America's Heartland,” said Mike McCoshen, Administrator of the Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation. AGLPA and its partners intend to use the findings to engage shippers, carriers and terminal operators in developing commercially viable freight movements. The central conclusion: significant opportunities exist without constructing new waterway connections, provided industry can better utilize those already in place. An Indian seafarer is missing and two others have been hospitalized after the Panama-flagged LPG tanker TARA GAS came under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz, forcing its 25-member crew to abandon ship. India’s Ministry of External Affairs said Tuesday that 21 of the 24 Indian nationals aboard had been safely evacuated ashore at Khasab, Oman, while two injured Indian crew members were admitted to a hospital. Search and rescue operations were continuing for the missing seafarer. The latest developments follow two tanker attacks reported Monday by UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) , both of which resulted in engine-room fires. According to UKMTO Warning 208-26 , a tanker was attacked at approximately 1900 UTC on November 16, about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman. The attack disabled the vessel and sparked an engine-room fire. The crew was initially reported safe. However, in an update issued Tuesday, UKMTO said a maritime security agency had reported a second strike against the vessel, causing another fire. At that time, the agency said the crew’s whereabouts were unaccounted for. India’s Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Sarbananda Sonowal, subsequently identified the vessel as TARA GAS , saying it had been targeted in a missile attack on November 16. In a subsequent statement , Sonowal confirmed that the tanker had suffered another attack and its entire crew had abandoned the vessel. “While 24 crew members have been safely accounted for, one Indian seafarer remains missing,” Sonowal said. Video circulating on social media purportedly shows a tanker engulfed in flames near the Strait of Hormuz, although gCaptain has not independently verified the footage. The Indian Embassy in Muscat said it was coordinating with Omani authorities on rescue operations and assistance to the surviving crew. The incident follows a separate attack earlier Monday, when the company security officer of another tanker reported that an unidentified projectile struck the vessel while it was transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz. That incident, recorded under UKMTO Warning 207-26 at 0558 UTC, also caused an engine-room fire. All crew members were accounted for, with no casualties initially reported. The attacks underscore the continuing dangers facing commercial shipping in the strategic waterway, where vessel movements remain severely disrupted by the conflict with Iran. The full extent of the damage to TARA GAS and any potential environmental impact remain unknown. Responsibility for the attacks has not been independently established. articles.body: GXO Logistics has announced new financial targets for 2030, outlining plans to increase revenue and profitability through its logistics operations, automation and artificial intelligence. The company presented its long-term strategy during its Investor Day at the New York Stock Exchange on 16 November 2026. The event focused on GXO’s growth priorities, financial performance and capital allocation plans. GXO is targeting annual organic revenue growth of more than 7% between 2027 and 2030. It also aims to achieve an adjusted EBITA margin above 6.5% by 2030. In addition, the company has set a free cash flow conversion target of 40% to 50% of adjusted EBITDA. The targets reflect GXO’s plans to expand its logistics services while improving operating efficiency. GXO outlines preliminary outlook for 2027 Alongside its long-term targets, GXO introduced preliminary financial guidance for 2027. The company expects organic revenue growth above 5.5% next year. Meanwhile, it is targeting an adjusted EBITDA margin above 7.1% and an adjusted EBITA margin exceeding 4.5%. According to GXO, the targets follow changes to its operating model and commercial strategy over the past year. The company is also focusing on technology, automation and artificial intelligence as part of its long-term development. “Our ambition is to lead the future of supply chain services in the next era of intelligent, AI-powered logistics and solve increasingly complex challenges for customers,” said Patrick Kelleher, CEO, GXO Logistics. Kelleher added that GXO has strengthened its business model and commercial approach while expanding its focus on advanced logistics technology. The financial targets come as the company continues investing in automation across its global warehouse network. GXO recently announced an expanded partnership with Apptronik to test humanoid robots in warehouse operations. The companies are exploring a potential deployment of up to 1,000 robots over the next four years, subject to successful trials and operational requirements. The initiative forms part of GXO’s broader efforts to integrate advanced robotics into logistics operations. GXO currently operates more than 1,000 facilities worldwide, covering over 200 million square feet of logistics space. The company employs more than 150,000 people and provides contract logistics services to customers across multiple industries. The newly announced targets establish GXO’s financial ambitions through the end of the decade. However, actual results will depend on market conditions, business performance and the company’s ability to implement its strategy.

SOFIA, Nov 17 (Reuters) – A liquefied petroleum gas tanker sank off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast on Tuesday, Bulgaria’s defense ministry said, a few dozen miles from where another ship went down after a drone attack a day earlier. The Liberian-flagged vessel, Gas Husky , sent a distress signal before sinking approximately 50 miles east of Byala, the ministry said. The Transport Ministry said that all 19 crew members had been evacuated from the life raft to an air base in the town of Varna. It said that the tanker was carrying 3,400 metric tons of liquefied petroleum gas at the time it sank. The vessel’s Greece-based manager did not respond immediately to a request for comment. articles.body: Vessels November 17, 2026 · 6 minutes ago Fourth floating LNG terminal put into operation mode to fuel Germany’s energy security Germany’s federally commissioned LNG terminal program is now complete, with four floating LNG terminals delivered in just four years. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 1 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Energos Force Source: DET In another step towards diversifying Germany's energy network to curb dependence on individual gas suppliers and transport routes, Deutsche Energy Terminal (DET), part of the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action and a state-owned operator of four liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals, has strengthened the country’s gas import flexibility and security of supply by commissioning its fourth and final federally commissioned terminal in Stade. Germany’s newly commissioned LNG terminal in Stade is expected to feed up to 3.2 billion cubic meters of natural gas into the national grid in 2027, which is equivalent, in theoretical annual heating demand, to around 2.6 million four-person households. The FSRU Energos Force will receive LNG from LNG carriers, regasify it on board, and feed it into the German gas grid. " With the LNG terminal in Stade, we are strengthening Germany’s energy supply and making it more independent and more resilient. In a challenging time, Lower Saxony took on responsibility and made an important contribution to putting the energy supply on a broader footing. Security of supply is the prerequisite for economic strength. At the same time, we are looking ahead: we need an energy infrastructure that provides security today and paves the way to a climate-neutral energy supply tomorrow. Stade is an important location for this. " — Olaf Lies Minister-President of the State of Lower Saxony Related Articles Fossil Energy Boost for Germany’s energy security comes with third LNG terminal up and running 4 min read The commissioning marks the completion of the country’s four-terminal floating LNG program, delivered by DET in four years, diversifying gas import routes. Aside from the new Stade site , Deutsche Energy Terminal operates two LNG terminals in Wilhelmshaven and one in Brunsbüttel . " With the LNG terminal in Stade, we are commissioning the fourth and final federally owned terminal. Four terminals in less than four years: this shows how quickly Germany can act when it matters. We have put our gas supply on a broader footing and are thus more independent of individual suppliers and transport routes. With the Energos Force, another import route is now being added that will strengthen our supply this winter already. In 2027, up to 3.2 billion cubic meters of natural gas are expected to be fed into the German gas grid via the Stade terminal. In theory, this corresponds to the annual heating energy demand of around 2.6 million four-person households. " — Katherina Reiche Federal Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy Related Articles Clean Fuel FSRU docks in Stade as LNG terminal prepares to feed gas into German grid from November 3 min read According to DET, these four terminals strengthen Germany’s security of supply and create additional options for importing natural gas independently of individual transport routes and supply structures. Having originally planned, permitted and built at several locations at once in an acute emergency, we now have, with the commissioning of the Stade site, four terminals for a secure and resilient energy supply for Germany. The Greater PAJ project encompasses the development of five offshore fields, including Palas, Astraea, Juno, Dione and Urano. articles.body: Exploration & Production November 17, 2026 · 2 minutes ago Shell kicks off gas production from its deepwater project in Southeast Asia Shell has brought online a natural gas development off the coast of Malaysia, which is home to an offshore platform designed to run on solar energy. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Rosmari-Marjoram topside sailaway Source: Malaysia Marine and Heavy Engineering Holdings (MHB) Sarawak Shell, a subsidiary of the UK-headquartered energy giant Shell, has begun flowing the first gas from its deepwater fields off Sarawak, Malaysia, which are expected to support the company's production growth into the 2030s. Shell has started production from the Rosmari and Marjoram fields located 220 kilometers off the coast of Sarawak, bringing its latest development on stream four years after making a final investment decision (FID) in 2022 to develop the project, containing these deepwater sour gas fields discovered in 2014. " Shell is proud of its long and successful history in Malaysia. We have strong expertise in this basin, and the start-up of Rosmari-Marjoram contributes to production growth into the 2030s. This project builds on decades of experience to bring new gas supply online efficiently and competitively. " — Peter Costello President of Upstream The company explains that the gas produced from Rosmari-Marjoram will be piped to a new onshore gas plant in Bintulu, Sarawak, where it will be processed and fed to the Petronas LNG Complex . The development consists of a subsea tie-back, an unmanned wellhead platform, a 207-kilometer pipeline to shore, and an onshore gas plant at Bintulu. The project’s offshore platform is powered by solar panels , with back-up diesel generators available when needed. The onshore plant draws on the predominantly hydropower-based local electricity grid, supplemented by renewable energy certificates to achieve 100% renewable power. Related Articles Fossil Energy Shell’s new solar-powered platform with 20-year design life on its way to offshore gas field (Gallery) 2 min read " The offshore platform is designed to be powered by solar panels when it is unmanned, with batteries providing storage for up to three days of electricity. Diesel generators provide a backup source of electricity and help to power the platform when personnel visit for maintenance, which requires more energy to run ancillary services. The onshore gas plant is run on the equivalent of 100% hydropower, with renewable energy certificates complementing hydropower used directly from the electricity grid. " — Shell elaborated. The firm drilled Malaysia’s first oil well in 1910 and has been producing gas offshore since 1982. In addition to Rosmari-Marjoram, the company has interests in multiple producing fields off the coast of Sarawak, including Timi and Gorek , and is exploring other potential opportunities in the basin. According to Shell, Rosmari-Marjoram contributes to its commitment to deliver upstream and integrated gas projects coming on stream between 2025 and 2030 with a total peak production of more than 1.4 million barrels of oil equivalent per day (boe/d). articles.body: Contracts & Tenders November 17, 2026 · 10 minutes ago ExxonMobil pushes ahead with Guyana’s eighth oil project as Saipem gets the all-clear and SBM Offshore bags FPSO job Guyana’s deepwater expansion is gaining momentum as ExxonMobil moves to the execution phase of its recently sanctioned offshore oil development. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Constellation Source: Saipem ExxonMobil Guyana, a subsidiary of the U.S.-headquartered energy giant ExxonMobil, has given Italy’s Saipem the go-ahead to proceed with the $1-1.5 billion subsea assignment on its eighth oil development project in the Stabroek block off the coast of Guyana and handed out a floating production, storage, and offloading (FPSO) award to the Netherlands-based SBM Offshore. Saipem has received the authorization to proceed with the execution of the Longtail project in Guyana’s Stabroek block, located at a water depth of approximately 1,750 meters. This comes shortly after ExxonMobil made a final investment decision (FID) for the eighth development on the offshore block and follows Saipem's announcement regarding the receipt of the limited notice to proceed (LNTP) in April 2026 to begin the preliminary activities for detailed engineering and procurement of long-lead equipment destined for the project. The contract, with an estimated overall value of between $1 billion and $1.5 billion, entails the engineering, procurement, construction, and installation (EPCI) of the subsea structures, umbilicals, risers, and flowlines (SURF) system. Following the receipt of the necessary government and regulatory approvals, as well as the FID for the project, the Italian giant is in the clear to continue with the execution of the remaining contract activities, with an expected duration of around four years. The company will perform offshore operations using vessels from its fleet, such as FDS2 , Castorone , and Constellation . Fabrication activities will be executed at Saipem's Italian yard in Arbatax, Sardinia, while logistics will be managed in Guyana through the Vreed-en-Hoop Shorebase Inc. (VEHSI) yard, involving the local supply chain and resources. “With the Longtail project, Saipem confirms its presence in a strategic country, where it has already been awarded seven offshore development contracts by ExxonMobil Guyana Limited, namely Liza Phase 1 and Phase 2, Payara, Yellowtail, Uaru, Whiptail and Hammerhead,” emphasized the Italian company. Related Articles Project & Tenders ExxonMobil reaches FID on eighth project offshore Guyana 2 min read Meanwhile, SBM Offshore has been awarded contracts by ExxonMobil Guyana for the same development project to construct and install an FPSO, which it expects to operate for an initial period of ten years, combining the strengths of both companies and leveraging the expertise, experience, and operational excellence of the FPSOs currently deployed in the Stabroek block. The award follows completion of front-end engineering and design (FEED) studies and the final investment decision on the project by the operator and its block co-venturers. The FPSO design is based on SBM Offshore’s Fast4Ward program, incorporating the company’s tenth new-build multi-purpose floater hull. The FPSO, which will be designed to produce and process 1.2 billion standard cubic feet of gas per day and 250,000 barrels of condensate per day, will be spread moored in a water depth of about 1,750 meters and able to store around 2 million barrels of condensate. " We are proud to receive this sixth FPSO award from ExxonMobil Guyana. This milestone demonstrates our strong collaboration with ExxonMobil and highlights the strength of our Fast4Ward program, which industrializes complex deepwater developments through standardized design, disciplined execution and the transfer of lifecycle learnings across our fleet. Combined with a culture of continuous improvement and a relentless pursuit of excellence, this approach allows us to continuously evolve our solutions, accelerate delivery and create lasting value for our clients. " — Øivind Tangen Chief Executive Officer of SBM Offshore Building on the experience gained from the FPSOs Liza Destiny , Liza Unity , Prosperity , One Guyana , and Jaguar , SBM Offshore emphasizes that it remains committed to supporting local content development in Guyana by expanding its collaboration with Guyanese companies, sourcing fabrication scope locally, and recruiting and integrating Guyanese engineers into both the execution and operational teams, including the FPSO project team. ExxonMobil Guyana operates the Stabroek block and has a 45% interest, with Hess Guyana Exploration, part of Chevron, owning 30%, and CNOOC Petroleum Guyana holding the remaining 25%. The latest set of awards follows on the heels of ExxonMobil’s start-up of Uaru , its fifth development in the Stabroek block, lifting the country’s installed production capacity to 1.1 million barrels per day. Join the leading maritime news network An aerial view shows the oil tanker named Boracay (also called Pushpa), a vessel being investigated by French authorities and suspected of belonging to the so-called "shadow fleet" involved in the Russian oil trade, off the coast of the western France port of Saint-Nazaire, France, October 2, 2025. REUTERS/Stephane Mahe The European Union has imposed a new round of sanctions targeting the shipowners, vessel managers, insurers and financial networks supporting Russia’s shadow fleet, expanding its efforts to disrupt the maritime infrastructure behind Russian oil exports. The measures announced Monday add 12 individuals and 101 entities to the EU’s sanctions list, including companies based in the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Seychelles and China that Brussels says are involved in transporting or trading Russian oil. The latest designations go beyond individual tankers to target the companies and people that own, manage, insure and finance their operations. Among those sanctioned are Russian nationals Igor Konfino and Daniil Mosin, identified by the EU as managers of White Agate Marine, Citrine Marine and Serpentine Marine, companies that own vessels already subject to European sanctions. According to the EU’s Official Journal , several of those vessels were previously owned by Russian shipping giant Sovcomflot or associated companies. The EU says the ownership and management structures maintain links to Sovcomflot while operating tankers engaged in high-risk shipping practices. The sanctions also target a network of Dubai-based companies involved in Russian oil transportation, including Lidoil DMCC, Spikoil DMCC, Lynx Ship Management, Stalwart Shipmanagement, Grace Shipmanagement and Greenlight Shipmanagement. EU officials say Lidoil manages tankers carrying Russian crude and petroleum products through shell companies, while Spikoil operates vessels on its behalf. The listings also expose financial connections supporting those operations. Moscow-based Lead Capital, an affiliate of Lidoil, was sanctioned for helping raise financing in Russia to support the tanker network. Marine insurance is another target. The EU designated Moscow-based Balance Insurance, which it says provided coverage to the oil tanker GARUDA , a vessel previously sanctioned over high-risk shipping practices while transporting Russian crude. The inclusion of an insurer highlights the broader effort to restrict the services that allow sanctioned tankers to remain in operation, even when individual vessels have already been blacklisted. Brussels also sanctioned JSC Petersburg Oil Terminal, which operates an oil terminal in the St. Petersburg region, extending the measures to infrastructure supporting Russia’s energy exports. The maritime designations form part of a wider sanctions package targeting Russia’s energy and financial sectors. Nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions were also added to the list as the EU seeks to limit Moscow’s access to financing. Under the measures, designated individuals and companies face asset freezes, while EU persons and businesses are prohibited from making funds or economic resources available to them, directly or indirectly. Listed individuals are also subject to EU travel bans.
